chapters.title: Learning Together
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the river speaks to jahnavi; jahnavi begins school; king bruce and the spider; perseverance and language skills.

lessons.title: The River Speaks to Jahnavi

activities.prompt: What might the river say if Jahnavi could ask it one question?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Jahnavi's Dreams
activities.body: Jahnavi was a bright and hopeful girl from a coastal village in India. Her parents worked on the farm, and she had three brothers. She dreamed of going to school and learning to read. Jahnavi wanted to understand nature's wonders. The River told her that it was hurrying towards the sea.
keyPoints: Jahnavi dreamed of going to school.
She wanted to learn and understand nature.
The River was moving towards the sea.
activities.explanation: This lesson introduces Jahnavi's dreams and the River's message.

activities.prompt: Why can Jahnavi's bright hope survive her mother's worry?
steps: Jahnavi wants to go to school because she wants to learn and understand nature.
Her mother delays this plan because she thinks Jahnavi is too small.
Jahnavi stays hopeful because she is bright and believes in her dream.
Therefore, her school dream is delayed, but she will likely keep hoping.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where did Jahnavi live?
options: In a coastal village in India
On a farm in a forest
In a city near the sea
In a village by a lake
activities.explanation: Jahnavi lived in a coastal village in India. The River spoke to her there.

activities.prompt: Jahnavi's mother said she was too small and might go to ______ later.
activities.hint: Jahnavi's dream was to learn there.
activities.explanation: Her mother said she was too small and might go to school later.

activities.prompt: Jahnavi dreamed of going to school.
activities.explanation: Her dream was to go to school. She hoped to learn there.

activities.prompt: How many brothers did Jahnavi have?
options: One brother
Two brothers
Three brothers
Four brothers
activities.explanation: Jahnavi had three brothers. She lived in a coastal village with her family.

activities.prompt: Match each person with the fact about them.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a person with the action described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: What did the River say about the moon?
options: The moon always stayed still
The moon travelled towards the sea
The moon moved away from the sea
The moon travelled towards the village
activities.explanation: The River said that the moon always travelled towards the sea. This was part of its message.

activities.prompt: Jahnavi hopes to go to school. Her mother says she is too small and might go later. How might Jahnavi feel?
options: She feels sad but still hopeful.
She feels happy and fully relaxed.
She feels angry and never hopeful.
She feels proud and ready to wait.

This mistake treats delayed school as a reason to feel happy.
This mistake ignores Jahnavi's bright and hopeful nature.
This mistake turns her wish for school into pride in waiting.

activities.explanation: Her school wish is delayed, but she remains hopeful.

activities.prompt: Jahnavi is nearly ten and looks after little Appu. What does this tell us about her?
options: She is caring and responsible.
She dislikes having little ones.
She wants to go far away.
She is afraid of all children.

This mistake reads looking after Appu as dislike.
This mistake connects family care with wanting to leave.
This mistake turns one caring act into fear of children.

activities.explanation: Looking after Appu shows that she is caring and responsible.

activities.prompt: The River says it must hurry towards the sea. The moon always travels towards the sea. What can we work out from this?
options: They move towards the same place.
They move with the very same speed.
They turn around before reaching sea.
They always travel towards different places.

This mistake confuses a shared place with a shared speed.
This mistake contradicts their stated movement towards the sea.
why.They always travel towards different pla: This mistake ignores that both travel towards the sea.

activities.explanation: Both the River and the moon travel towards the sea.

activities.prompt: Jahnavi wants to read like Ettan and Meena. She also wants to understand nature's many wonders. Why does she want to learn?
options: To gain knowledge and understand more.
To win prizes and earn much praise.
To avoid all work and rest daily.
To copy others without asking why.

This mistake connects learning with prizes and praise.
This mistake connects learning with avoiding work.
This mistake confuses learning with copying without understanding.

activities.explanation: Her wishes show that she wants knowledge and a deeper understanding.

activities.prompt: Jahnavi's parents work on the farm. Her mother says she is too small for school and might go later. What can we work out?
options: Her school dream is strong but delayed.
Her school dream is weak and fading.
Her parents already sent her to school.
Her mother thinks school is completely wrong.

This mistake treats a delay as proof that her dream is fading.
This mistake confuses speaking about school with attending it.
why.Her mother thinks school is completely w: This mistake turns her mother's worry about age into rejection of school.

activities.explanation: Jahnavi strongly wants school, but her mother delays her.

lessons.title: Jahnavi Begins School

activities.prompt: What would help Jahnavi find the courage to enter school?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Jahnavi Goes to School
activities.body: The River told Jahnavi that her feet would become wet if she went by it. It advised her to slip into the school and listen. It said little girls could do as much as little boys. Jahnavi feared the children, but she gathered courage and went to school. The teacher promised to discuss her schooling with her father.
keyPoints: The River advised Jahnavi to slip into the school and listen.
Jahnavi gathered courage and went to school.
The teacher promised to discuss Jahnavi’s schooling with her father.
activities.explanation: Jahnavi listened to advice and took the step to school.

activities.prompt: Jahnavi is afraid to go to school. How does she face this fear?
steps: The River tells Jahnavi to slip into the school and listen.
This helps because she can hear if the teacher will let her stay.
She is still afraid because children may frighten and chase her away.
Still, she gathers courage and goes to the school, overcoming that fear.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The River’s Advice
activities.prompt: What did the River advise Jahnavi to do?
options: Slip into the school and listen.
Slip into the school and leave.
Go past the school and wait.
Ask the teacher to leave.
activities.explanation: The River advised Jahnavi to slip into the school and listen.

activities.prompt: The River said little girls could do as much as little boys.
activities.explanation: The River said that little girls could do as much as little boys.

activities.title: Who Said or Did What?
activities.prompt: Match each person or source with the correct action or words.
pairs: Slip into the school and listen
Take Jahnavi to see a ship
Discuss Jahnavi’s schooling with her father
The teacher might let Jahnavi stay
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a person or source with what they said or did.

activities.title: Jahnavi’s Fear
activities.prompt: What did Jahnavi fear would happen at school?
options: The children would frighten and chase her away.
She was afraid of a lizard or a snake.
She was afraid her teacher would send her home.
She was afraid the river would turn away.
activities.explanation: Jahnavi feared that the children would frighten and chase her away.

activities.title: Jahnavi Takes a Step
activities.prompt: What did Jahnavi do after hearing the River?
options: She gathered courage and went to school.
She stayed by the river and waited.
She asked Chandu to take her home.
She hid near the school all day.
activities.explanation: Jahnavi gathered courage and went to the school.

activities.title: Jahnavi’s Journey
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Jahnavi feared the children.
The River pointed out her lack of fear.
Jahnavi gathered courage.
Jahnavi went to the school.
activities.explanation: Jahnavi first feared the children, then gathered courage and went to school.

activities.prompt: The River tells Jahnavi to slip into the school and listen. What good might come from listening?
options: The teacher may let Jahnavi stay in school.
She may learn how the river makes boats.
She may find the school beside a ship.
She may hear children telling her to leave.

This wrongly thinks the river makes boats.
This wrongly puts a ship beside the school.
why.She may hear children telling her to lea: This wrongly thinks listening will lead to being sent away.

activities.explanation: This is right because the River hopes the teacher may let her stay.

activities.prompt: Chandu says he can take Jahnavi to see a ship. A child sees one on the water. What is the child seeing?
options: A boat that is much larger than usual.
A small animal that lives close to water.
A school building beside the river.
A lizard that is hiding near a boat.

why.A small animal that lives close to water: This mistakes a large boat for a small animal.
This mistakes a boat on the water for a school building.
This mistakes a large boat for a hiding lizard.

activities.explanation: This is right because the story describes ships as very large boats.

activities.prompt: Jahnavi is not afraid of a lizard or snake. Why does the River point this out?
options: The River wants her to try school despite fear.
The River wants her to fear every river animal.
The River wants her to avoid all children.
The River wants her to stay beside the river.

why.The River wants her to fear every river: This wrongly turns the comparison into advice to fear animals.
why.The River wants her to avoid all childre: This wrongly treats the comparison as advice to avoid children.
why.The River wants her to stay beside the r: This wrongly assumes the River wants Jahnavi to stay there.

activities.explanation: This is right because it helps Jahnavi face her school fear.

activities.prompt: The teacher promises to discuss Jahnavi's schooling with her father. What does this suggest will happen?
options: The teacher will hear her father's wishes about school.
The teacher will send her away without any discussion.
The teacher will let her stay without asking.
The teacher will ask the river to choose for her.

why.The teacher will send her away without a: This wrongly treats the promise as an immediate rejection.
why.The teacher will let her stay without as: This wrongly assumes the teacher will not discuss it with her father.
why.The teacher will ask the river to choose: This wrongly assumes the river will make the choice.

activities.explanation: This is right because discussing schooling includes hearing her father's wishes.

activities.prompt: The River says little girls can do as much as little boys. Jahnavi's mother supports girls' education. What shared idea do they support?
options: Girls can learn and go to school.
Girls should learn only beside boys.
Girls should stop going to school.
School belongs only to little boys.

This wrongly limits girls' learning to boys.
This wrongly turns support for girls into a demand to stop learning.
This wrongly claims that only boys belong at school.

activities.explanation: This is right because both ideas support girls learning at school.

lessons.title: King Bruce and the Spider

activities.prompt: What helped King Bruce keep trying when he felt like giving up?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A spider gives hope
activities.body: King Bruce was Scotland’s monarch and wore a crown. He wanted to do a great deed for his people. Although he tried many times, he could not succeed. He became very sad and felt like giving up. A spider appeared while he was thinking. Its brave example gave him hope to try again.
keyPoints: King Bruce wanted to do a great deed.
He felt like giving up after repeated failure.
The spider’s persistence encouraged him to try again.
activities.explanation: The spider’s persistence helps King Bruce find hope.

activities.prompt: A task feels hard, and you fail many times. What should you do next?
steps: First, King Bruce wanted to do a great deed for his people.
His many failures made him sad because he felt like giving up.
The spider showed him why trying again can lead to success.
Therefore, try once more instead of giving up when you fail.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did King Bruce wear?
options: A crown
A spider
A web
A robe
activities.explanation: King Bruce wore a crown as Scotland’s monarch.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the story with its meaning.
pairs: Doing a great deed for his people
Falling and trying to climb again
Feeling very sad and wanting to give up
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a wish, a struggle, or a feeling from the story.

activities.prompt: Why did the spider keep climbing?
options: To reach its web
To wear a crown
To leave Scotland
To gain a throne
activities.explanation: The spider had a long climb ahead because it wanted to reach its web.

activities.prompt: After praising the spider, King Bruce decided to try ______.
activities.hint: The spider never stopped trying.
activities.explanation: The spider’s efforts encouraged King Bruce to try again.

activities.prompt: Put the main events in the correct order.
items: King Bruce felt like giving up
A spider appeared
King Bruce praised the spider
King Bruce decided to try again
King Bruce succeeded
activities.explanation: The spider’s example helps King Bruce decide to try again and succeed.

activities.prompt: What happened after King Bruce decided to try again?
options: He succeeded when he tried again.
He failed when he tried again.
The spider ruled Scotland instead.
He asked the spider for help.
activities.explanation: King Bruce succeeded when he tried once more.

activities.prompt: The spider kept climbing after it fell. What did King Bruce learn from this?
options: That spiders are royal rulers
That he should remove his crown
That only spiders can succeed
That he should try again

why.That spiders are royal rulers: This wrongly treats the spider as a royal ruler.
why.That he should remove his crown: This wrongly makes his crown part of his decision.
why.That only spiders can succeed: This wrongly limits success to spiders, while King Bruce succeeded.

activities.explanation: This is right because the spider's example encouraged him to try again.

activities.prompt: The spider often fell but tried again. It made nine attempts and one more. What kind of creature does this show?
options: A weak and careless creature
A lonely and frightened creature
A brave and determined creature
A selfish and proud creature

why.A weak and careless creature: This mistakes falling for weakness, but the spider tried again.
why.A lonely and frightened creature: This confuses trying again with loneliness or fear.
why.A selfish and proud creature: This confuses its effort to reach home with selfishness or pride.

activities.explanation: This is right because repeated tries after falling show bravery and determination.

activities.prompt: The spider fell and tried again. A child falls while learning to ride. What should the child do next?
options: Stop riding for the whole day
Give up riding after this fall
Blame the bicycle for the fall
Try again with a brave heart

why.Stop riding for the whole day: This mistakes one fall for a reason to stop trying.
why.Give up riding after this fall: This repeats the wrong idea that failure should end the effort.
why.Blame the bicycle for the fall: This wrongly treats the fall as someone else's fault.

activities.explanation: This is right because the spider's example shows the value of trying again.

activities.prompt: King Bruce praised the spider and tried once more. What did his success show?
options: His crown made him succeed alone
The spider did his great deed
He could succeed despite earlier failures
He knew the answer from the start

why.His crown made him succeed alone: This wrongly treats his crown as the cause of his success.
why.The spider did his great deed: This wrongly says the spider completed King Bruce's deed.
why.He knew the answer from the start: This mistakes later success for knowing the answer from the beginning.

activities.explanation: This is right because he succeeded once more after earlier failures.

lessons.title: Perseverance and Language Skills

activities.prompt: How can a tiny ant discover the power of never giving up?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Never Give Up
activities.body: Perseverance means keeping on even when something is difficult. The poem tells King Bruce’s story in a narrative style. A metaphor compares unlike things without needing ‘like’, ‘as’ or ‘as...as’. It strengthens the poem’s message about never giving up. The ant and bird also show the power of trying again and working together.
keyPoints: Perseverance means never giving up.
A narrative style tells a story.
A metaphor strengthens the poem’s message.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect stories and word choices with perseverance.

activities.prompt: A child sees the ant facing a heavy crumb. What can the ant’s story teach the child?
steps: The ant and her friends work together.
They can lift the crumb because they join their efforts.
Their success shows that teamwork helps with difficulty.
The clear lesson is to keep trying and never give up.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Ant and the Bird
activities.body: The bird kept trying until it built a strong nest. The ant was inspired by the bird’s success. The ant and her friends worked together to lift the crumb. The ant story teaches us never to give up. In a letter about overcoming difficulty, use transition words.
keyPoints: The bird kept trying until it succeeded.
The ant and her friends worked together.
A difficult letter should use transition words.
activities.explanation: The bird and ant show how determination and working together help.

activities.prompt: Match each word or phrase with its meaning.
pairs: Tells the story of King Bruce
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a word or phrase with its meaning.

activities.prompt: The poem uses a narrative style to tell King Bruce’s story.
activities.explanation: The poem tells the story of King Bruce in a narrative style.

activities.prompt: What inspired the ant to try?
options: The bird’s success
The ant’s determination
The spiders’ group
The poem’s message
activities.explanation: The ant was inspired by the bird’s success.

activities.prompt: Spiders belong to a group called ______.
activities.hint: Use the group name given for spiders.
activities.explanation: Spiders belong to a group called the arachnids.

activities.prompt: Which reason best explains the metaphor’s job in the poem?
options: It strengthens the perseverance message.
It identifies King Bruce’s story.
It names the spiders’ group.
It describes the bird’s nest.
activities.explanation: The metaphor strengthens the poem’s message about perseverance.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen in the story.
items: The bird kept trying.
The bird built a strong nest.
The ant was inspired.
The ant and her friends worked together.
activities.explanation: The bird’s success inspired the ant, who then worked with her friends.

activities.prompt: The bird keeps trying and builds a strong nest. The ant sees this success. The ant starts her task with hope. What does this show?
options: The bird’s success inspired her.
The bird’s success worried her.
The bird’s success confused her.
The bird’s success ended her effort.

This mistake thinks success makes someone stop trying.
This mistake thinks success creates worry instead of hope.
This mistake thinks success ends effort instead of inspiring it.

activities.explanation: The ant acted because the bird’s success inspired her.

activities.prompt: A poem says, ‘The ant’s courage was a flame.’ The ant’s courage and a flame are unlike things. What does the line do?
options: It makes an implied comparison.
It makes a plain explanation.
It tells a short story.
It joins two separate ideas.

This mistake treats a metaphor as a literal explanation.
This mistake confuses a metaphor with a narrative style.
This mistake confuses a metaphor with a transition word.

activities.explanation: It compares unlike things without using like or as.

activities.prompt: A poem says, ‘Her hope burned inside her.’ No word like or as appears. What can the poem still do?
options: It can compare unlike things.
It can explain two plain facts.
It can tell a longer story.
It can join two ideas.

This mistake treats a metaphor as a plain explanation.
This mistake confuses comparison with telling a story.
This mistake thinks transitions are needed for comparisons.

activities.explanation: The poem can still compare unlike things.

activities.prompt: The ant and her friends pull at a crumb. They lift it by working together. What does their success teach?
options: Teamwork can help them succeed.
The crumb can pull them upward.
The bird must help every ant.
One ant can lift any crumb.

This mistake treats the crumb as an active helper.
This mistake adds the bird to the ant’s helping team.
This mistake forgets that the friends shared the work.

activities.explanation: Working together helps the ant and her friends lift the crumb.

lessons.title: Helen Keller’s Three Days

activities.prompt: What wonders might Helen Keller discover during her three remarkable days?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Helen Keller’s Three Days
activities.body: Helen Keller found many interesting things through touch alone. She felt the delicate symmetry of a leaf, the rough bark of a pine tree, and a singing bird’s movement. She wanted very much to see beautiful things. Over three days, she wished to see her supporters, rise with the dawn, see museums, and watch people in the city.
keyPoints: Helen discovered many things through touch.
She wanted very much to see beautiful things.
Her wishes were connected with people, dawn, museums, and city life.
activities.explanation: Helen used touch to explore, while her wishes centred on seeing the world around her.

activities.prompt: A child cannot see a leaf, a pine tree, or a singing bird. How can Helen understand them?
steps: Helen learns much through touch because it reveals many interesting things.
She feels a leaf's delicate symmetry because touch reveals its shape.
She feels rough pine bark and bird movement because touch gives details.
Her strong wish to see shows that touch cannot end her longing.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did Helen use to discover many interesting things?
options: Touch alone
Sight alone
Reading alone
Guessing alone
activities.explanation: Helen found many interesting things through touch alone.

activities.prompt: Helen felt the delicate symmetry of a leaf.
activities.explanation: Yes, Helen felt the delicate symmetry of a leaf.

activities.prompt: Helen described the rough bark of a ______ tree.
activities.hint: Think of the tree named in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Helen described the rough bark of a pine tree.

activities.prompt: When did Helen want to rise with the dawn?
options: On the first day
On the second day
On the third day
After the third day
activities.explanation: On the second day, Helen wanted to rise with the dawn.

activities.prompt: Match each wish with the correct day.
pairs: See the people who supported her
activities.explanation: Each wish belongs to the day named in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put Helen’s three wishes in the correct order.
items: First day: see the people who supported her
Second day: rise with the dawn
Third day: observe people in the city
activities.explanation: The wishes happened on the first, second, and third days.

activities.prompt: What did Helen want to see in the museums?
options: The pageant of human progress
The delicate symmetry of leaves
The movement of a singing bird
The rough bark of trees
activities.explanation: She wanted to see the pageant of human progress in the museums.

activities.prompt: What did Helen advise people to do?
options: Use their eyes as if they might soon lose their sight
Keep their eyes closed at all times
Use their ears instead of their eyes
Wait until their sight is gone
activities.explanation: Helen advised people to value their eyes while they still had their sight.

activities.prompt: Helen wanted to see those who supported her. What did this show?
options: She wanted to avoid the people who helped her.
She wanted them to stop helping her.
She cared about the people who helped her.
She did not value the people who helped her.

why.She wanted to avoid the people who helpe: This mistake thinks her wish meant she wanted to avoid them.
This mistake thinks she wanted their support to end.
why.She did not value the people who helped: This mistake thinks wanting to see them showed she did not value them.

activities.explanation: This is right because she wanted to see the people who supported her.

activities.prompt: She wanted to see human progress in museums. What did she hope?
options: That museums should remain empty.
That progress did not matter to people.
That people had made great advances.
That people had stopped moving forward.

This mistake sees a museum visit as wanting no museum displays.
This mistake thinks human progress meant progress did not matter.
This mistake reverses the meaning of human progress.

activities.explanation: This is right because human progress means people had moved forward.

lessons.sceneCaption: Helen Keller experiences a statue through touch.

lessons.title: Senses, Inclusion and Communication

activities.prompt: How could we explore the world with senses beyond sight?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Our senses and inclusion
activities.body: Helen invited people to enjoy music, birdsong and the sounds of an orchestra. She also asked them to touch objects, because touch might soon fail. Sensory words describe how we see, hear, smell, taste or feel. Modal verbs show necessity, possibility, permission or ability. Braille uses raised dots for letters. A screen reader reads text shown on a screen. Inclusion needs the right tools and the right mindset.
keyPoints: Sensory words describe our experiences.
Braille and screen readers support communication.
Inclusion needs tools and the right mindset.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect our senses with communication and inclusion.

activities.prompt: Your little brother says he will always hear and touch. So he does not need to enjoy them now. Is he right?
steps: Helen asked people to enjoy music, birdsong and orchestras, so she thought sounds were worth listening to.
She asked people to touch things as if touch might soon fail, so she thought touch could be lost.
She called sight the most delightful sense, so she thought our senses bring great joy.
So your brother is wrong, because we should enjoy our senses now, not later.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which sounds did Helen ask people to enjoy?
options: Music and birdsong
Music and touch
Birdsong and touch
Orchestra sounds and touch
activities.explanation: Music and birdsong were two sounds Helen asked people to enjoy.

activities.prompt: Sensory words describe how we ______, hear, smell, taste or feel something.
activities.hint: It names one of the ways we use our senses.
activities.explanation: Sensory words describe how we experience something through our senses.

activities.prompt: Match each idea to its meaning.
pairs: Reads text displayed on a screen
The right tools and the right mindset
activities.explanation: Raised dots represent letters. Screen readers read displayed text. Inclusion needs tools and the right mindset.

activities.prompt: In “touch might soon fail”, what does “might” show?
options: Necessity
Possibility
Permission
Ability
activities.explanation: “Might” shows possibility. It tells us that touch could fail, not that it must fail.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the order they happen.
items: Text is displayed on a screen
A screen reader reads the text
Visually impaired people use digital services independently
activities.explanation: The text appears first. The screen reader reads it. Independent digital use follows.

activities.prompt: A visually impaired person uses digital services independently. Which idea explains inclusion?
options: Tools and an inclusive mindset
An inclusive mindset alone
Tools without an inclusive mindset
Neither tools nor mindset
activities.explanation: Inclusion needs both the right tools and the right mindset.

activities.prompt: A library sign says, 'You must return this book today.' A boy reads it and runs home. Why does he run?
options: The sign says it is only possible
The sign says it is necessary
The sign gives him permission
The sign says he is able to

why.The sign gives him permission: Permission is about being allowed, which 'must' does not show.
why.The sign says he is able to: Ability is about being able to, not being forced to.

activities.explanation: Must shows necessity, so he knows he has to go.

activities.prompt: Louis became blind young after an accident. Why did he make letters from raised dots?
options: So letters would look pretty on paper
So people could read them with their eyes
So children could count the dots for fun
So blind people could read by touch

why.So letters would look pretty on paper: Looking pretty is about sight, which blind people cannot use.
why.So people could read them with their eye: Reading with eyes is exactly what blind people cannot do.
why.So children could count the dots for fun: Counting dots for fun does not help anyone read letters.

activities.explanation: Raised dots can be felt, so blind people can read them.

She would have to stop looking after Appu.
She would need to leave the coastal village.
She would lose interest in reading and nature.

why.She would have to stop looking after App: Looking after Appu does not necessarily prevent her from attending school.
why.She would need to leave the coastal vill: There is no reason given that she must leave the village.

activities.context: Jahnavi is a bright, hopeful girl with three brothers in a coastal village in India. Her parents work on the farm, and she dreams of going to school. Measure the moon’s brightness instead of its movement.
Choose whichever direction seems more hopeful.
Accept the statement without checking because the River said it.

why.Choose whichever direction seems more ho: Hopefulness is not a way to check a direction.
why.Accept the statement without checking be: Trusting the words alone would not provide a check.

She wants to read like Ettan and Meena.
She wants to understand nature’s wonders.
Her mother thinks she should wait to attend school.

activities.context: Jahnavi was afraid that the schoolchildren would frighten her and chase her away. The River advised her to slip inside and listen, and it hoped the teacher might let her stay. activities.prompt: Jahnavi has entered the school. What should she do next?
options: Leave at once, because the other pupils will certainly drive her away.
Listen to the lesson and let the teacher decide whether she may remain.
Run outside and ask Chandu to show her a large boat instead.
Wait silently without listening until the teacher has discussed her schooling with her father.

why.Leave at once, because the other pupils: Jahnavi’s fear may happen, but it is not certain.
why.Run outside and ask Chandu to show her a: Chandu’s offer does not help her decide what to do inside the school.
why.Wait silently without listening until th: The teacher will discuss schooling with her father, but listening should come first.

activities.explanation: This follows the River’s advice to listen and consider the teacher’s decision.

activities.context: Jahnavi was afraid that the schoolchildren would frighten her and chase her away. The River advised her to slip inside and listen, and it hoped the teacher might let her stay. Since little girls could do as much as little boys, Jahnavi gathered courage and entered the school. The teacher promised to discuss Jahnavi’s schooling with her father, and Jahnavi’s mother supported girls’ education.
activities.prompt: Why was Jahnavi able to try entering the school despite her fear?
options: The River reminded her that girls were as capable as boys and that she did not fear a lizard or a snake.
Chandu’s promise to show her a ship made the school seem less frightening.
Jahnavi knew that her father had already agreed to her schooling.
Her mother’s support convinced her that the children could not frighten her.

why.Chandu’s promise to show her a ship made: The ship had no connection to entering the school.
why.Jahnavi knew that her father had already: The teacher still had to discuss Jahnavi’s schooling with her father.
why.Her mother’s support convinced her that: Her mother’s support did not remove Jahnavi’s fear of the children.

Stay long enough to hear the lesson and give the teacher a chance to decide.
Ask Chandu to take her to see a ship before she speaks to the teacher.
Immediately announce that girls are as capable as boys and demand that she remain.

why.Run out before hearing what the teacher: Running away would prevent her from following the River’s advice.
why.Ask Chandu to take her to see a ship bef: Chandu’s offer does not answer the problem inside the school.
why.Immediately announce that girls are as c: An immediate demand replaces listening with an argument.

activities.context: King Bruce, Scotland’s monarch, wanted to do a great deed for his people. He tried many times but failed, so he became sad and felt like giving up. A spider appeared. The spider had to climb a long way to its web. It often fell but tried again, making nine brave attempts and one more upward climb. Finally, it entered its web. King Bruce praised the spider, decided to try again, and succeeded when he tried once more.
activities.prompt: If King Bruce had given up as soon as he felt sad, what would probably have happened?
options: He might not have tried again and so might not have succeeded.
He would have succeeded during one of his earlier attempts.
He would have continued trying even though he had decided to give up.
He would have reached the same success without the spider’s example.

why.He would have succeeded during one of hi: The story says that his earlier attempts did not succeed.
why.He would have continued trying even thou: Saying he had given up conflicts with continuing to try.
why.He would have reached the same success w: The spider’s example was linked to his decision to try again.

activities.explanation: Giving up would have ended his efforts before the attempt that succeeded.

activities.context: King Bruce, Scotland’s monarch, wanted to do a great deed for his people. He tried many times but failed, so he became sad and felt like giving up. A spider appeared. The spider had to climb a long way to its web. It often fell but tried again, making nine brave attempts and one more upward climb. Finally, it entered its web. King Bruce praised the spider, decided to try again, and succeeded when he tried once more.
activities.prompt: What should King Bruce do after failing many times, based on what the spider did?
options: Make another attempt, using the spider’s persistence as encouragement.
Give up because many failures prove that success is impossible.
Wait for the spider to complete the deed for his people.
Try only when he feels completely certain that he will succeed.

why.Give up because many failures prove that: Many failures do not prove that success is impossible.
why.Wait for the spider to complete the deed: The spider encouraged King Bruce; it did not complete his deed.
why.Try only when he feels completely certai: Waiting for complete certainty could prevent him from making the attempt that succeeded.

activities.explanation: This follows the spider’s example of continuing after failure.

activities.prompt: How does the spider’s experience show the difference between giving up and continuing?
activities.answer: The spider fell many times but kept making attempts, including nine brave tries and one more. It finally entered its web. King Bruce had tried many times without success, yet the spider’s persistence persuaded him to try again, and this time he succeeded.
points: The spider kept trying despite falling.
It made nine brave attempts and one more.
The spider reached its web.
King Bruce was inspired to continue and succeeded.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A class explored how the poem tells King Bruce’s story and how its metaphor strengthens the message about perseverance. In the ant story, a bird kept trying until it built a strong nest. The ant, known for her determination, was inspired by the bird’s success. The ant and her friends worked together to lift a crumb. A student planned a letter about overcoming difficulty and was reminded to use transition words.
activities.prompt: If the bird had stopped before building a strong nest, which result would be most likely?
options: The ant might have had less encouragement from the bird’s success.
The ant might have been inspired by the bird’s decision to stop.
The bird might have continued trying after the ant gave up.
The ant might have lifted the crumb without her friends.

why.The ant might have been inspired by the: The case says the bird’s success inspired the ant, not its decision to stop.
why.The bird might have continued trying aft: This reverses the roles: the bird persisted, while the ant received encouragement.
why.The ant might have lifted the crumb with: The case shows that the ant and her friends worked together to lift the crumb.

activities.explanation: Correct: Without the bird’s success, the ant would lose the stated source of encouragement.

activities.context: A class explored how the poem tells King Bruce’s story and how its metaphor strengthens the message about perseverance. In the ant story, a bird kept trying until it built a strong nest. The ant, known for her determination, was inspired by the bird’s success. The ant and her friends worked together to lift a crumb. activities.prompt: Which sentence best uses a transition word to connect a difficulty with a lesson about never giving up?
options: I faced a difficulty, and I kept trying.
When I faced a difficulty, I kept trying. Therefore, I learned to continue.
I faced a difficulty. I kept trying. It was difficult.
I faced a difficulty. Then I kept trying. The difficulty was difficult.

This joins the events with “and” instead of using a transition word.
why.I faced a difficulty. I kept trying. It: No transition word connects the events, and the word “difficult” is repeated.
why.I faced a difficulty. Then I kept trying: “Then” shows order, but the final sentence does not clearly express the lesson.

activities.explanation: Correct: “Therefore” clearly connects the effort with the lesson learned.

activities.prompt: How does the ant story support the poem’s message about perseverance?
activities.answer: The ant story shows perseverance through the bird’s persistence and the ant’s determination. The bird kept trying until it built a strong nest. Inspired by that success, the ant and her friends worked together to lift the crumb. Their actions show that encouragement and cooperation can help someone overcome difficulty and never give up.
points: The bird kept trying until it built a strong nest.
The bird’s success inspired the ant.
The ant and her friends worked together to lift the crumb.
Their actions support the message of never giving up.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

Stop exploring because the bark no longer matched her expectation.
Wait until she could see the bark with her eyes.
Describe the movement of the nearby singing bird instead.

why.Stop exploring because the bark no longe: An unexpected texture would not end her curiosity.
why.Wait until she could see the bark with h: Her wish to see does not replace touch.
why.Describe the movement of the nearby sing: The bird is separate from the pine tree.

activities.context: Helen Keller stands beside a pine tree, feeling its rough bark while holding a leaf and listening to a singing bird nearby. Use touch alone whenever possible.
Save your eyesight for a time when it may be gone.
Ignore the importance of beautiful things.

why.Save your eyesight for a time when it ma: She does not advise waiting until sight is lost.
why.Ignore the importance of beautiful thing: She deeply values seeing beautiful things.

activities.answer: Helen uses touch to discover details. She feels a leaf’s delicate symmetry, the rough bark of a pine tree, and a singing bird’s movement. points: She felt the leaf’s delicate symmetry.
She felt the pine tree’s rough bark.
She felt the singing bird’s movement.
She still valued sight.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

It feels the raised dots and speaks the letters it finds.
It turns the words on the screen into speech she can hear.
It works out the answer and tells her what to write.

why.It feels the raised dots and speaks the: Raised dots are felt by fingers, not by software.
why.It works out the answer and tells her wh: It reads the page out; it does not supply answers.

activities.context: At break, the class visits the library. Because she thought touch was more delightful than sight.
Because she wanted them to give up using their eyes.
Because she was sure their sense of touch would fail one day.

why.Because she wanted them to give up using: She never asked anyone to stop seeing; she asked them to touch.
why.Because she was sure their sense of touc: 'Might' means it could happen; she did not say it certainly would.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between how the raised-dot book and the screen reader give a student words?

activities.prompt: How does Dr. Dolittle learn to talk with animals?

activities.title: Learning Animal Language
activities.body: Doctor Dolittle can learn animal language. Polynesia teaches him bird words, and he eagerly writes them down. Parrots can speak both people’s language and bird language. Their words can ask whether the porridge is hot. Animals communicate through different parts of their bodies. Dogs use their noses to ask questions. Dolittle becomes famous among animals all over the world.
keyPoints: Polynesia teaches Dolittle bird words.
Animals communicate through different body parts.
Dolittle learns to speak with animals.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how Dolittle learns from animals and uses animal language.

activities.prompt: How can a dog ask a question without using words?
steps: Animals use different body parts because each part can send a message.
A dog's nose asks questions, so noses send animal messages.
Doctor Dolittle learns animal language, so he can understand animal messages.
He can answer animals because he understands how they communicate.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Animals Tell Dolittle Things
activities.body: Animals can communicate through different parts of their bodies. Dogs use their noses to ask questions. A plough horse tells Doctor Dolittle that he needs spectacles for one blind eye. Dolittle makes separate doors for different kinds of animals. He learns animal language well enough to speak with animals himself. He gives up being a people’s doctor altogether.
keyPoints: Dogs use their noses to ask questions.
A plough horse needs spectacles for one blind eye.
Dolittle makes separate doors for different animals.
He gives up being a people’s doctor.
activities.explanation: Animals use different ways to communicate with Dolittle.

Polynesia
Doctor Dolittle
The plough horse

activities.prompt: Polynesia says parrots can speak people’s language and bird language. She teaches Dolittle bird words that ask whether the porridge is hot. Why does Dolittle eagerly write down these bird words?

He wants to hide all people’s words from birds.

why.He cannot walk through the stable door w: This mistake mixes seeing with walking.

why.Animals can stop visiting him through ev: This mistake ignores that the doors help animals visit.

activities.title: Animals, Words, and Care
activities.body: Sick animals tell Doctor Dolittle where their pain is and how they feel. A compound word joins two words of different parts of speech. Bird language has a space. Flowerpots has no space. Cat’s-food-Man has hyphens. The present perfect uses has or have with a past participle. Ayurveda is India's oldest medical system. Animals received good medicinal care in ancient India. Strays may need food, water, or an animal shelter.
keyPoints: Sick animals show Dolittle their pain and feelings.
Compound words can use spaces, no spaces, or hyphens.
Strays may need food, water, or an animal shelter.

Take it to an animal shelter because this is another suggested way.

Together, food, water, shelter, and treatment can help the animal.

activities.title: Playful Words and Funny Verses
activities.body: Phrasal verbs join a verb with a preposition or adverb. The two parts work as one unit. Sometimes, their meaning differs from the separate words. A limerick is a funny, nonsensical verse with five lines. The limericks here follow AABBA. The funny man represents humour, imagination, and rule-breaking.

A limerick has five lines and follows AABBA.
The funny man represents humour, imagination, and rule-breaking.

activities.prompt: A sign at a building site says "Look out!" Your cousin reads it and starts looking out of the window. Why is he wrong?
steps: "Look out" is a phrasal verb, so the two words work as one unit, not two.
A phrasal verb can mean something different from its two words, so here it does not mean "look outside".
It really means "be careful", so the cousin should watch for falling things, not the window.
So he should read "look out" as one warning word, and that is why his looking out is wrong.

activities.title: Before the Guests Arrive
activities.body: Mary is a girl who needs to learn how to speak politely. Mrs. Shaw asks her to put her coat away and keep the room tidy. Mary changes into a clean dress. Mrs. Shaw says kindness is the best way to say the right thing. She tells Mary to restart a conversation and ask guests to stay longer. Mary forgets her mother’s advice when the guests arrive, making it humorous.

Use kindness and start conversations again.
Ask guests to stay a little longer.

activities.prompt: Mary feels nervous when guests arrive. What should she remember?
steps: Mary should use kindness, because Mrs. Shaw says it is the best way.
She should start the conversation again, because this gives guests a way to join in.
She should ask guests to stay longer, because this gives the conversation more time.
So Mary should be kind, keep talking, and invite guests to stay longer.

activities.prompt: What does Mary do before the guests arrive?
options: Change into a clean dress
Put Mrs. Shaw’s coat away
Leave her coat in the hall
Talk whenever she wants

Start the conversation again

activities.explanation: Kindness guides the right words, followed by restarting the talk and inviting a longer stay.

activities.prompt: Why is the play humorous?
options: Mary forgets her mother’s advice
Mrs. Shaw asks for a tidy room
Mary wears a clean dress
Mary learns to speak politely
activities.explanation: Mary forgets her mother’s advice when the guests arrive.

activities.prompt: Mrs. Shaw says Mary leaves clothes everywhere. How might Mary feel?

She may feel angry because she likes the mess.
She may feel happy because nobody noticed.
She may feel proud because clothes belong outside.

why.She may feel angry because she likes the: Anger mistakes Mrs. Shaw's concern for a complaint about Mary's choice.
why.She may feel happy because nobody notice: Happiness misses the untidy house that Mrs. Shaw mentions.
why.She may feel proud because clothes belon: Pride wrongly treats leaving clothes as something to celebrate.

activities.explanation: Embarrassment fits because Mrs. Shaw says the house looks untidy.

activities.prompt: The play is humorous when Mary forgets her advice. Why?
options: It shows that a forgotten lesson can create humor.
It shows that guests always forget important advice.
It shows that mothers should never give advice.
It shows that untidy rooms always make people laugh.

why.It shows that guests always forget impor: This wrongly says that the guests forget the advice, not Mary.
why.It shows that mothers should never give: This wrongly treats the mistake as a reason to avoid advice.
why.It shows that untidy rooms always make p: This wrongly says that untidy rooms cause the humor.

activities.explanation: This is right because the humor comes from forgetting the mother's advice.

activities.prompt: Mrs. Harding is Mr. Harding's wife. Mrs. Lee is his sister. How are they related?

They are strangers who meet at the same party.
They are neighbors because they share a front gate.
They are both married to the same man.

why.They are strangers who meet at the same: This wrongly ignores the family connection that Mrs. Lee has.
why.They are neighbors because they share a: This wrongly turns a family connection into a neighbor connection.
This wrongly makes Mrs. Lee another wife of Mr. Harding.

activities.explanation: This is right because Mrs. Lee is Mr. Harding's sister.

activities.prompt: Mrs. Shaw asks Mary to put her coat away and tidy. Mary changes into a clean dress before guests arrive. Why might she do both?

To avoid speaking to anyone politely.
To show that she dislikes having guests.

This wrongly connects neat clothes with avoiding polite speech.
This wrongly suggests that neat clothes show dislike for guests.

activities.explanation: This is right because both actions help Mary look neat for the guests.

lessons.title: Say the Right Thing: The Visit and Language Learning

activities.prompt: What might Mary learn about choosing kinder words during her visit?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What the Visit Teaches Us
activities.body: During a visit, Mary speaks unkindly. She tells Mrs. Harding something untrue and criticises Mr. Best and Mrs. Cotter. She calls Mrs. Grantley talkative and calls a dog dirty and unwanted. When the guests leave, Mary says the wrong farewell. Suffixes are word endings added to root words. “Say” focuses on the message. “Tell” focuses on the receiver. Intonation is the rise and fall of pitch while speaking.
keyPoints: Mary says the opposite of what she should say when the guests leave.
Suffixes are word endings added to root words.
“Say” focuses on the message; “tell” focuses on the receiver.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the visit and three useful language ideas.

activities.prompt: What should Mary do differently during her visit?
steps: Mary says she saw Mrs. Harding’s children, but she did not.
This is wrong because Mrs. Harding receives a false message.
Mary criticises the guests and reverses her goodbye.
Therefore, she should give true messages because each listener must receive them well.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Suffixes are word ______ added to root words.
activities.hint: They are added at the end of a word.
activities.explanation: The lesson calls suffixes word endings added to root words.

activities.prompt: Mary has truly seen Mrs. Harding's children.
activities.explanation: Mary wrongly tells Mrs. Harding that she has seen her children.

activities.prompt: What does Mary wrongly criticise Mrs. Cotter for?
options: staying in bed and calling a doctor
using a train and meeting a banker
praising her children and meeting Mr. Best
visiting Mrs. Grantley and praising a dog
activities.explanation: Mary criticises Mrs. Cotter for staying in bed and calling the doctor.

activities.prompt: Match each comment to the person or dog.
pairs: Claims she has seen the children
Staying in bed and calling the doctor
Calling the dog dirty and unwanted
activities.explanation: Each comment shows which person or dog Mary was criticising.

activities.prompt: Put these moments in order.
items: Mary criticises Mr. Best and Mrs. Cotter.
The guests leave.
Mary says the opposite of what she should say.
activities.explanation: Mary's criticisms come before the guests leave. Her wrong farewell comes afterwards.

activities.prompt: Why is Mary's goodbye at the end wrong?
options: It says the opposite of the right words.
It repeats Mr. Best's train routine again.
It praises Mrs. Grantley's talking loudly.
It changes “say” into “tell” at once.
activities.explanation: The lesson says Mary says the opposite of what she should say.

activities.prompt: Mary tells Mrs. Harding that she has seen her children. How does Mrs. Harding most likely feel?
options: She feels misled because Mary has not seen her children.
She feels pleased because the visit has been friendly.
She feels bored because her children are not there.
She feels surprised because Mary is talking about the train.

why.She feels pleased because the visit has: This mistakes a false statement for friendly talk.
why.She feels bored because her children are: Children being absent does not show that Mrs. Harding feels bored.
why.She feels surprised because Mary is talk: Talking about the train does not explain her feelings about her children.

activities.explanation: Mary has not seen the children, so Mrs. Harding receives false information.

activities.prompt: Mr. Best explains his train routine to Mary. Mary says bankers cannot think. What is Mary doing?
options: She is insulting his work and dismissing bankers’ thinking.
She is helping him improve his train routine.
She is praising bankers because she wants to join them.
She is explaining why doctors should stay in bed.

why.She is helping him improve his train rou: Criticising the routine does not show that Mary is helping him.
why.She is praising bankers because she want: Mary criticises bankers, so she is not praising them.
why.She is explaining why doctors should sta: The doctor and bed belong to Mrs. Cotter’s situation, not Mr. Best’s.

activities.explanation: Calling bankers unable to think insults Mr. Best’s work.

activities.prompt: Mrs. Cotter stays in bed and calls the doctor. Mary criticises both actions. What does this show about Mary?
options: She judges Mrs. Cotter’s actions instead of showing care.
She supports Mrs. Cotter’s choices and helps her rest.
She changes Mrs. Cotter’s train routine for the better.
She praises the doctor because Mrs. Cotter called him.

why.She supports Mrs. Cotter’s choices and h: Mary criticises Mrs. Cotter, so this is not support.
why.She changes Mrs. Cotter’s train routine: The train routine is Mr. Best’s, not Mrs. Cotter’s.
why.She praises the doctor because Mrs. Cott: Mary criticises the call, so she is not praising the doctor.

activities.explanation: Mary criticises both actions, so she is judging instead of caring.

activities.prompt: Mary calls Mrs. Grantley talkative and says such women are not interesting. How might Mrs. Grantley feel?
options: She may feel hurt because Mary rejects her conversation.
She may feel happy because Mary wants to hear more.
She may feel calm because the doctor has been called.
She may feel excited because Mary praises her silence.

why.She may feel happy because Mary wants to: Mary rejects conversation, so happiness is not supported.
why.She may feel calm because the doctor has: The doctor belongs to Mrs. Cotter’s situation, not this one.
why.She may feel excited because Mary praise: Mary criticises Mrs. Grantley, so she is not praising her silence.

activities.explanation: Mary calls her talkative and uninteresting, which can hurt her feelings.

activities.prompt: Mary calls the dog dirty and unwanted. At leaving, she says the opposite of what she should say. What should Mary think about first?
options: She should think about the message each listener receives.
She should think about the word endings added to roots.
She should think about the rise and fall of tone.
She should think about the train routine before speaking.

why.She should think about the word endings: Suffixes change word endings, not the meaning of Mary’s judgement.
why.She should think about the rise and fall: Intonation changes pitch, but Mary’s problem is her message.
why.She should think about the train routine: Mr. Best’s train routine does not guide the dog or goodbye message.

activities.explanation: “Say” focuses on the message, and the listener must receive it correctly.

activities.prompt: A learner joins the ending “-ing” with the root “play”. A speaker’s pitch rises and falls. Which explanation fits both changes?
options: The first change adds a suffix, and the second shows intonation.
The first change shows intonation, and the second adds a suffix.
The first change adds a message, and the second shows a receiver.
The first change shows a root, and the second adds an ending.

why.The first change shows intonation, and t: This swaps the two language ideas instead of matching each change.
why.The first change adds a message, and the: Messages and receivers do not describe a word ending or changing pitch.
why.The first change shows a root, and the s: The root is already there, and changing pitch is intonation.

activities.explanation: A suffix is added to a root, and intonation is the rise and fall of pitch.

activities.prompt: Why does Doctor Dolittle eagerly write down the bird words Polynesia teaches him?
options: He can remember bird words for later conversations with birds.
Only the question about hot porridge is useful enough for him to record.
He wants to show that bird language and people’s language are identical.
He plans to prevent Polynesia from giving him further lessons.

why.Only the question about hot porridge is: One example does not limit the usefulness of all bird words.
why.He wants to show that bird language and: Similar communication does not mean the languages are identical.
why.He plans to prevent Polynesia from givin: Eagerness to write does not mean rejecting more lessons.

activities.explanation: Writing down the words helps him use them later.

activities.context: Polynesia taught Dolittle the language of birds, including a question about whether porridge was hot. Dolittle eagerly wrote down her lessons and soon could talk with animals himself. During one visit, the plough horse said that spectacles were needed for one blind eye. The Cat’s-food-Man said Dolittle understood animals better than local vets. Dolittle then gave up people’s doctor work. He made a separate door for every kind of animal, and he became famous among animals all over the world.
activities.prompt: If a dog approaches and uses its nose to ask a question, what should Doctor Dolittle do next?
options: Reply using animal language so the dog can understand him.
Ask Polynesia to turn the nose signal into bird words.
Tell the dog to repeat the question in people’s language.
Show the dog its separate door instead of answering the question.

why.Ask Polynesia to turn the nose signal in: Polynesia teaches words but is not described as translating every signal.
why.Tell the dog to repeat the question in p: The dog’s question should be answered rather than changed into another language.
why.Show the dog its separate door instead o: A separate door helps with entry but does not answer the question.

activities.explanation: Dolittle can speak with animals himself.

activities.prompt: How does Polynesia’s teaching help Dolittle learn to speak with animals?
activities.answer: Polynesia explained that parrots can speak both people’s language and bird language. She taught Dolittle bird words, including a question about whether porridge is hot. Dolittle eagerly wrote down what she taught him and learned animal language well enough to speak with animals himself.
points: Polynesia explains the two languages spoken by parrots.
She teaches Dolittle bird words, including the porridge question.
Dolittle eagerly records the words she teaches.
He learns enough animal language to speak with animals himself.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child finds a stray animal near 12, Rose Lane, Woodstock, where an animal clinic announcement is displayed. The child considers giving the animal meals and water or taking it to a shelter. The child also reads about Doctor Dolittle, whose garden attracts many creatures seeking treatment, and learns how animals can show where pain is and how they feel. In language, the child notes “cat’s-food-man,” “bird language,” and “flowerpots,” then uses “has” or “have” with a past participle.
activities.prompt: After finding the stray animal, what should the child do?
options: Provide food and water, and arrange for the animal to go to an animal shelter.
Provide only food and water, because taking the animal to a shelter would not help.
Take the animal to an animal shelter, but give it no food or water before leaving.
Give the animal food and water, then take it to the clinic even if it has no illness.

why.Provide only food and water, because tak: This wrongly dismisses the shelter suggestion.
why.Take the animal to an animal shelter, bu: This wrongly leaves out the need for food and water.
why.Give the animal food and water, then tak: This confuses the animal clinic with the suggested shelter arrangement.

activities.explanation: Both caring for the animal and finding it a shelter are suggested actions.

activities.context: A child finds a stray animal near 12, Rose Lane, Woodstock, where an animal clinic announcement is displayed. The child considers giving the animal meals and water or taking it to a shelter. The child also reads about Doctor Dolittle, whose garden attracts many creatures seeking treatment, and learns how animals can show where pain is and how they feel. In language, the child notes “cat’s-food-man,” “bird language,” and “flowerpots,” then uses “has” or “have” with a past participle.
activities.prompt: Which sentence correctly describes what the child has done?
options: The child has given the animal food and water.
The child have given the animal food and water.
The child has give the animal food and water.
The child has giving the animal food and water.

why.The child have given the animal food and: “Have” does not agree with the singular subject “the child.”
why.The child has give the animal food and w: A past participle is needed after “has,” not the base verb.
why.The child has giving the animal food and: “Giving” is not a past participle and cannot follow “has” in this form.

activities.explanation: “Has” is followed correctly by the past participle “given.”

activities.context: At a school fancy-dress day, a boy copies the funny man. He balances a shoe on his head and puts two hats on his feet. When a teacher greets him, he is polite, then offers her a currant bun instead of a flower and holds it to her nose. She steps back against the wall. He sits on the ground and sings. She asks why he wears two hats on his feet; he hops home on his head.
activities.prompt: The teacher steps back against the wall. Which explanation best fits what happened?
options: The bun was pushed so close to her face that she moved away before she had decided to.
She wanted to leave the room quietly because the boy had started singing.
She was moving towards the wall to help steady the shoe on the boy's head.
She had already told the boy to stand further away from her.

why.She wanted to leave the room quietly bec: Wrong cause: the singing comes later and nothing says it moved her.
why.She was moving towards the wall to help: Wrong: the shoe is on his head, not something she was holding up.
why.She had already told the boy to stand fu: Wrong: it swaps who acted; she moves, and no request is mentioned.

activities.explanation: Right: her body reacted to the bun being held near her nose.

activities.context: At a school fancy-dress day, a boy copies the funny man. He balances a shoe on his head and puts two hats on his feet. When a teacher greets him, he is polite, then offers her a currant bun instead of a flower and holds it to her nose. She steps back against the wall. He sits on the ground and sings. She asks why he wears two hats on his feet; he hops home on his head.
activities.prompt: A classmate wants to copy the funny man in a school show, but the teachers must stay comfortable. What should the classmate do?
options: Keep the strange costume and the hopping, but offer the bun without pushing it into anyone's face.
Give up the whole act, because odd behaviour of any kind is not allowed in school.
Keep every action exactly the same, since copying a poem can never cause a problem.
Replace the funny behaviour with a serious poem so that nobody laughs.

why.Give up the whole act, because odd behav: Too strict: the case shows the behaviour is playful, not forbidden.
why.Keep every action exactly the same, sinc: Too careless: it repeats the one action that caused the trouble.
why.Replace the funny behaviour with a serio: Overcorrects: it throws away the humour the poem is built on.

activities.explanation: Right: it keeps the humour and removes only the part that made someone step back.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the funny man's behaviour and the way people usually behave when they meet someone?
activities.answer: Usually a person shakes hands or offers a flower and keeps a polite distance. The funny man does the opposite in small ways: a shoe on his head, hats on his feet, a bun instead of a rose, and a hop home on his head. Yet he stays polite throughout.
points: Usual behaviour: a greeting such as a handshake or a flower, at a comfortable distance.
His actions are the reverse: shoe on his head, hats on his feet, a bun instead of a rose.
He ends by hopping home on his head rather than walking.
The politeness itself is not reversed; only his actions are odd.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In an English class, a group of students is preparing a funny turn for the school assembly. They write a five-line verse about a boy who 'gives up' his homework and 'puts off' his bath. On stage the actors take turns walking, staggering and hopping. Their teacher says the verse must be funny and nonsensical, and that the actors remind her of street performers.
activities.prompt: A classmate suggests changing 'puts off' to 'puts on' so the line sounds different. What would the group most likely expect to happen?
options: The line keeps its meaning, because the verb itself has not changed.
The meaning changes, because the same verb with a different preposition can carry a different meaning.
The line stops being a phrasal verb and becomes a single word.
The meaning changes only if the actor changes his movement as well.

why.The line keeps its meaning, because the: The verb alone does not fix the meaning; the small word attached to it helps decide it.
why.The line stops being a phrasal verb and: A phrasal verb stays two words; it never fuses into one word.
why.The meaning changes only if the actor ch: Acting and movement have nothing to do with what the words mean.

activities.explanation: Correct: swapping the preposition can give the same verb a different sense.

activities.context: In an English class, a group of students is preparing a funny turn for the school assembly. They write a five-line verse about a boy who 'gives up' his homework and 'puts off' his bath. On stage the actors take turns walking, staggering and hopping. Their teacher says the verse must be funny and nonsensical, and that the actors remind her of street performers.
activities.prompt: On the day of the assembly the actors all walk in the same way from start to finish. Why would the teacher say the turn no longer works?
options: Because the funny man is shown through varied, unusual movement, and one plain walk takes that away.
Because a limerick needs every actor to move in exactly the same way.
Because walking is a phrasal verb and cannot be acted out.
Because street performers are only compared to the funny man when they stand still.

why.Because a limerick needs every actor to: The sameness of the acting has no bearing on the verse's rhyme rules.
why.Because walking is a phrasal verb and ca: Walking is an ordinary verb, not a phrasal verb, and it can be performed.
why.Because street performers are only compa: The comparison to street performers comes from unusual behaviour, not from stillness.

activities.explanation: Correct: walking, staggering and hopping are offered as different ways of moving.

activities.prompt: Explain why the meaning of 'puts off' cannot be worked out just by adding the meanings of 'puts' and 'off'.
activities.answer: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a preposition or adverb, and the two words work as one unit. The whole unit can mean something its separate words do not, so adding 'puts' to 'off' may give the wrong idea. Using a different preposition can also change the meaning.
points: A phrasal verb is a verb with a preposition or adverb.
The words work as one unit.
Its meaning can differ from the meanings of its separate words.
The same verb with a different preposition can mean something else.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: How does the difference between “say” and “tell” help a learner understand Mary’s words to Mrs. Harding?
activities.answer: “Say” focuses on the message, while “tell” focuses on the person receiving it. In “Mary wrongly tells Mrs. Harding that she has seen her children,” the focus is on Mrs. Harding as the receiver. Knowing this difference helps a learner consider both the message and who receives it.
points: “Say” is linked to the message.
“Tell” is linked to the receiver.
Mary’s statement is identified as “tell”.
The learner considers the message and the receiver.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

lessons.title: The Burglar Alarm Begins

activities.prompt: What clever invention might turn an ordinary afternoon into an unexpected adventure?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Anand's New Scheme
activities.body: Anita, a fourteen-year-old girl, tells this story about her younger brother Anand. He thinks of himself as a scientist and enjoys tinkering with electrical gadgets. Tinkering means making and adjusting gadgets. His inventions usually do not work as intended. After many thefts, Anand decides that the colony needs a burglar alarm. He starts his latest scheme when his parents go out. A scheme is a plan.
keyPoints: Many thefts lead Anand to plan a burglar alarm.
Anand starts his scheme after his parents leave.
Anand enjoys making and adjusting electrical gadgets.
activities.explanation: Anand is an inventive boy who plans to help his colony.

activities.prompt: A colony has many thefts. What should Anand do to help protect it?
steps: Many thefts show that the colony needs better protection.
A burglar alarm can warn people when thieves enter.
Anand enjoys gadgets and has prepared a detailed alarm drawing.
So he should build and test the alarm because his inventions often fail.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Tells the Story?
activities.prompt: Who tells this story?
options: Anita, a fourteen-year-old girl
Papa, going to the office
Ma, going to the market
Anand, starting his scheme
activities.explanation: Anita tells the story. She is a fourteen-year-old girl.

activities.title: What Did Anand Decide?
activities.prompt: What did Anand decide that the colony needed?
options: a new bicycle for the colony
a burglar alarm
a taller gate for the colony
a brighter light for the colony
activities.explanation: Many thefts had taken place, so Anand decided the colony needed a burglar alarm.

activities.title: Anita's New Task
activities.prompt: Anita became involved in the scheme even though she wanted to finish her ______.
activities.hint: This is what Anita was writing.
activities.explanation: Anita joined Anand's scheme, although she wanted to finish her novel.

activities.title: Anand's Inventions
activities.prompt: What usually happens to Anand's inventions?
options: They always work exactly as Anand plans
They do not work as intended
They usually work better than he expects
They often work for many other people
activities.explanation: Anand usually does not get the intended result from his inventions.

activities.title: Why Was Papa Soaked?
activities.prompt: Why was Papa soaked?
options: because he always opened the door softly
because he opened the door as loudly as he could
because he forgot to return home from the office
because Ma went to the market that day
activities.explanation: Papa was soaked because he always opened the door softly.

activities.title: Put the Events in Order
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Papa left for the office while Ma went to the market.
Anand began his latest scheme.
Anand showed Anita a detailed drawing of the alarm.
activities.explanation: Anand began the scheme after his parents left. He then showed Anita the alarm drawing.

activities.prompt: Anita sees Anand's detailed alarm drawing. Why does she join his scheme?
options: She becomes interested in the alarm plan.
She thinks the drawing is a finished novel.
She expects her parents to return with tools.
She wants Anand to stop drawing gadgets.

why.She thinks the drawing is a finished nov: This mistake treats an alarm drawing as part of her novel.
why.She expects her parents to return with t: This mistake adds a visit by her parents that the facts do not give.
This mistake assumes Anita dislikes gadget plans.

activities.explanation: This is right because joining shows that the alarm plan interests Anita.

activities.prompt: The colony has many thefts. What should Anand's burglar alarm do?
options: Warn the colony when thieves enter.
Help Anand become a better story writer.
Show Anita how to draw electrical gadgets.
Tell Papa and Ma about Ma's market trip.

This mistake confuses the alarm with Anand's writing work.
why.Show Anita how to draw electrical gadget: This mistake confuses the alarm with Anand's detailed drawing.
This mistake confuses the alarm with a message about shopping.

activities.explanation: This is right because the alarm is meant to help against thefts.

activities.prompt: Anand calls his alarm work a scheme. What does scheme mean here?
options: A plan to make something work.
A tool that warns about thieves.
A picture of an electrical gadget.
A test of a failed invention.

This mistake confuses his plan with the finished warning tool.
This mistake confuses his plan with the drawing that explains it.
This mistake treats the scheme as a test of an old failure.

He copies Papa's office work at home.
He helps Ma finish shopping instead.
He leaves the colony problem to Anita.

This mistake confuses helping at home with helping Ma shop.
This mistake reverses the roles because Anand began the alarm plan.

activities.explanation: This is right because he uses a gadget plan to answer the theft problem.

activities.prompt: How could a home alarm be clever yet still fail its family?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Alarm and the Time Machine
activities.body: Anand rigged the alarm to work only when the door opened gently. It was designed for a burglar opening the door gently. When the alarm rang, a water bag fell on the thief’s head. Anand planned to call the police, while Anita asked him to clean the mess. Anita had doubts about identifying a burglar. The family watched a film about a time machine, and Anand decided to make one.
keyPoints: The alarm only worked when the door opened gently.
A water bag fell after the alarm started ringing.
The film led Anand to decide on making a time machine.
activities.explanation: The gentle-opening rule explains the alarm’s main problem.

activities.prompt: Why might Anand’s alarm go off without identifying a burglar?
steps: Anand set the alarm for a burglar opening the door gently.
Because any gentle opening can trigger it, the alarm cannot know the opener.
So it may ring loudly and make the water bag fall.
Anita’s doubt shows that it fails to identify the burglar.

options: The alarm
The police
The thief
The door

activities.prompt: Anand tried out a new invention for a week.
activities.explanation: Anand did not try out any new invention for a week.

activities.prompt: What did Anand plan to do after the alarm went off?
options: Clean the mess
Call the police
Watch the film
Make a time machine

activities.prompt: Anita asked Anand to clean the ______ before anyone returned home.

A burglar alarm
A time machine
Anand’s invention

He will hide the alarm in the house.
He will clean the fallen water mess.

To make Anand test a new invention.
To help the alarm ring much louder.

Wrong, because no new invention is linked to this cleaning request.

items: Collected parts

why.He is looking for his father’s hidden ke: This mistake connects every loud sound with the key.

He threatened Anita and Anand to remain quiet.
Anand tricked Boppa into entering his room.
Anand believed Boppa had started his time machine.

Anand’s trick put Boppa in his room, not Papa’s room.
This moved danger away from Papa’s room, showing Anand’s aim.
The crash and scream showed what happened after the trick.
