lessons.title: The Missing Boppa

activities.prompt: How did Boppa disappear without anyone finding him?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Search for Boppa
activities.body: Sharma Uncle and the neighbours unlocked the door. The adults entered Anand’s room cautiously and turned on the lights. The time machine was humming softly. Boppa’s green scarf was found near the switches. The neighbours checked how Boppa could leave and searched the house, but they could not find him. Boppa was never seen again. Anand still believed his time machine had worked, while Papa thought it was unsafe.
keyPoints: The neighbours searched for Boppa.
Boppa’s green scarf was found near the switches.
Anand and Papa had different thoughts about the machine.
activities.explanation: This shows the search, the missing Boppa, and the different beliefs about the machine.

activities.prompt: Why did the neighbours keep looking for Boppa after finding his scarf?
steps: The scarf gave them a clue, but it did not show where Boppa was.
They checked the ways out because they wanted to understand his absence.
They searched the house because Boppa might still be inside.
Since Boppa was never found or seen again, he remained missing.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Happened Next?
activities.body: The search moved from the room to the whole house. The neighbours checked how Boppa could leave, then searched everywhere inside. They could not find him anywhere, and he was never seen again. The green scarf was found near the switches. Anand continued to believe that his time machine had worked. Papa, however, thought the machine was unsafe and had it dismantled.
keyPoints: The neighbours searched the whole house.
Boppa was never seen again.
Papa had the machine dismantled because he thought it was unsafe.
activities.explanation: These details bring together the search and the ending.

activities.title: Before Entering the Room
activities.prompt: What did the neighbours do before the adults entered Anand’s room?
options: Turned on the lights
Unlocked the door
Checked how Boppa could leave
Searched the house
activities.explanation: The neighbours unlocked the door before the adults entered Anand’s room.

activities.title: The Scarf Clue
activities.prompt: Boppa’s green scarf was found near the switches.
activities.explanation: Yes. Boppa’s green scarf was found near the switches.

activities.title: Find the Missing Word
activities.prompt: Boppa’s ______ scarf was found near the switches.
activities.hint: It is a colour.
activities.explanation: The scarf was green, and it was found near the switches.

activities.title: Match the Details
activities.prompt: Match each clue or event with its matching detail.
pairs: The time machine was humming softly
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a clue or event with the detail given about it.

activities.title: The Search in Order
activities.prompt: Put the neighbours’ actions in the order they happened.
items: The neighbours unlocked the door
The adults entered Anand’s room and turned on the lights
The neighbours checked how Boppa could leave the house
The neighbours searched the house
activities.explanation: They opened the door, entered and lit the room, checked how Boppa could leave, then searched the house.

activities.title: Anand’s Belief
activities.prompt: What did Anand continue to believe?
options: That Boppa was still inside
That his time machine had worked
That the machine was unsafe
That the scarf was missing
activities.explanation: Anand kept believing that his time machine had worked. Papa thought it was unsafe.

activities.title: Papa’s Decision
activities.prompt: Papa had the machine dismantled because he thought it was safe.
activities.explanation: False. Papa had it dismantled because he thought it was unsafe.

activities.prompt: The neighbours enter Anand’s room carefully and turn on the lights. How do they feel?
options: They feel cautious because something may be wrong.
They feel excited because the room is dark.
They feel angry because the lights failed.
They feel playful because everyone is nearby.

why.They feel excited because the room is da: This mistake assumes that darkness causes excitement.
why.They feel angry because the lights faile: This mistake assumes that the lights failed, but they turned them on.
why.They feel playful because everyone is ne: This mistake treats careful movement as a playful feeling.

activities.explanation: Carefully entering the room shows that they felt cautious.

activities.prompt: The neighbours check every way out after Boppa vanishes. What are they trying to work out?
options: How Boppa could have left the house.
Why Anand wanted a time machine.
Why the neighbours needed green scarves.
Why the house needed more lights.

This mistake thinks they are checking Anand’s wish for a machine.
This mistake confuses Boppa’s search with a need for scarves.
This mistake treats their search as a lighting problem.

activities.explanation: Checking the ways out helps them understand how Boppa left.

lessons.title: Language, Inventions and Inventors

activities.prompt: How can sounds, clever ideas, and brave dreamers change our world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: New Words, New Ideas
activities.body: An onomatopoeia uses words that imitate actual sounds. A binomial is an expression made from two linked words. An idiom has a meaning different from the literal meanings of its words. Creativity means thinking new things. Innovation means doing new things. An invention brings ideas or objects together in a novel way to create something new.
keyPoints: Onomatopoeia imitates actual sounds.
Binomials join two linked words.
Creativity leads to innovation and invention.
activities.explanation: Great start! These words describe sounds, expressions, and new ideas.

activities.prompt: Anand has a new idea. How can he turn it into something new?
steps: He uses creativity to think of the idea, because creativity means thinking new things.
He then tries a new action, because innovation means doing new things.
He joins ideas or objects in a novel way, because this can create something new.
The result is an invention, because an invention brings ideas or objects together in a new way.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Important Contributions
activities.body: Sushruta’s innovations in surgery helped modern surgery develop. Dr Janaki Ammal made an important contribution to cytogenetics. ISRO launched the satellite Rohini into near-Earth orbit. Dr Narinder Singh Kapany played an important part in inventing fibre optics. An invention brings ideas or objects together in a novel way.
keyPoints: Sushruta’s innovations helped modern surgery develop.
Dr Janaki Ammal contributed to cytogenetics.
ISRO launched Rohini, while Dr Kapany helped invent fibre optics.
activities.explanation: These people and organisations made important new contributions.

activities.prompt: What makes an expression a binomial?
options: Words that imitate sounds
Two linked words
Meaning unlike literal words
New things brought together
activities.explanation: Yes! A binomial is an expression made from two linked words.

activities.prompt: Innovation means ______ new things.
activities.hint: Choose an action word from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Correct! Creativity means thinking new things, while innovation means doing them.

activities.prompt: Match each language or creativity word with its meaning.
pairs: Uses words that imitate actual sounds
Expression made from two linked words
activities.explanation: Well done! You matched each word with its lesson meaning.

activities.prompt: What is special about the meaning of an idiom?
options: A meaning unlike its literal words
A meaning made from linked words
A meaning based on actual sounds
A meaning shown by experiments
activities.explanation: Correct! An idiom means something different from its literal words.

activities.prompt: Put the steps in the lesson’s description of an invention.
items: Bring ideas or objects together
Join them in a novel way
Create something new
activities.explanation: Excellent! The lesson describes invention as joining ideas or objects in a new way.

activities.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a person with their work?
options: Sushruta — surgery innovations
Dr Janaki Ammal — fibre optics
Dr Narinder Singh Kapany — Rohini
ISRO — cytogenetics contribution
activities.explanation: Correct! Sushruta’s innovations in surgery helped modern surgery develop.

activities.prompt: Anand made a mess while trying new ideas. Anita asked Anand to clean it up. Why did Anita ask him?
options: She wanted him to take responsibility for the mess.
She wanted him to think of a new idea.
She wanted him to try another experiment.
She wanted him to leave the mess there.

This mistake confuses responsibility with creative thinking.
why.She wanted him to try another experiment: This mistake confuses responsibility with experimental work.
This mistake reverses the meaning of taking responsibility.

activities.explanation: Right: Anita wants Anand to take responsibility for the mess.

activities.prompt: A jar label says 'salt and pepper'. The two words are linked and work together. Why is this a binomial expression?
options: It joins two linked words as one expression.
It copies the sound of falling salt.
It gives a hidden meaning beyond each word.
It names one thing without any linked words.

This mistake confuses a binomial with copied sound.
why.It gives a hidden meaning beyond each wo: This mistake confuses a binomial with a hidden meaning.
why.It names one thing without any linked wo: This mistake says a binomial has no linked words.

activities.explanation: Right: two linked words work together as one expression.

activities.prompt: After a game, a child said, 'We are not sitting ducks now.' The team will defend itself. What does the idiom mean?
options: We are ready to defend ourselves.
The ducks are sitting beside us.
We are planning to leave now.
The game has already ended.

This mistake uses the literal meaning of the words.
This mistake treats the idiom as a plan to leave.
This mistake reads the game result into the idiom.

activities.explanation: Right: the literal meaning is not the intended meaning.

activities.prompt: A child first thinks of a new way to open a box. Next, the child tries a new action. Finally, two ideas are joined to make something new. Which order of words is correct?
options: Creativity, innovation, invention.
Innovation, creativity, responsibility.
Responsibility, invention, creativity.
Invention, innovation, creativity.

This mistake swaps creativity with innovation.
This mistake uses responsibility for creative thinking.
This mistake puts invention before creative thinking.

activities.explanation: Right: thinking new things comes first in this order.

activities.prompt: Sushruta’s innovations helped modern surgery develop. Dr Janaki Ammal made an important contribution to cytogenetics. ISRO launched Rohini into near-Earth orbit. Dr Narinder Singh Kapany helped invent fibre optics. Why are these examples in the lesson?
options: The examples cover several different areas of work.
The examples all belong to one single area of work.
The examples all describe one single kind of invention.
The examples all belong to one narrow field of study.

why.The examples all belong to one single ar: This mistake assumes one field can include all four examples.
why.The examples all describe one single kin: This mistake treats different achievements as one invention.
why.The examples all belong to one narrow fi: This mistake lets the satellite example hide the other fields.

activities.explanation: Right: the four examples cover clearly different areas of work.

activities.context: Many thefts had recently taken place in Anita’s colony. Her fourteen-year-old brother Anand saw himself as a scientist and enjoyed tinkering with electrical gadgets, though his inventions usually did not work as intended. He decided the colony needed a burglar alarm. When Papa left for the office and Ma left for the market, Anand began his scheme and showed Anita a detailed drawing. Anita joined despite wanting to finish her novel. Papa was soaked because he always opened the door softly.
activities.prompt: If Anand’s alarm behaves like his inventions usually do, what should Anita expect?
options: It may fail to give the protection Anand intended.
It will certainly give exactly the protection Anand intended.
It will work, but the colony will face even more thefts.
It will work, but only because Anita wanted to finish her novel.

why.It will certainly give exactly the prote: Certain success contradicts his usual record.
why.It will work, but the colony will face e: A working gadget does not necessarily cause more thefts.
why.It will work, but only because Anita wan: Anita’s writing wish does not determine whether the gadget works.

activities.explanation: This matches Anand’s usual pattern of unsuccessful inventions.

activities.context: Many thefts had recently taken place in Anita’s colony. Her fourteen-year-old brother Anand saw himself as a scientist and enjoyed tinkering with electrical gadgets, though his inventions usually did not work as intended. He decided the colony needed a burglar alarm. When Papa left for the office and Ma left for the market, Anand began his scheme and showed Anita a detailed drawing. Anita joined despite wanting to finish her novel. Papa was soaked because he always opened the door softly.
activities.prompt: Why was Papa soaked in the situation described?
options: The case connects his quiet manner at the entrance with getting wet.
His habit of opening the entrance forcefully was the reason given.
His journey to the office was the reason given.
His interest in electrical gadgets was the reason given.

why.His habit of opening the entrance forcef: He was described as opening the door softly, not forcefully.
why.His journey to the office was the reason: The office trip states where he went, not why he was soaked.
why.His interest in electrical gadgets was t: Tinkering explains Anand’s interest, not Papa’s condition.

activities.explanation: This matches the stated cause without copying the passage wording.

activities.prompt: Explain how Anand’s idea of himself and his habit of tinkering influenced the burglar-alarm scheme.
activities.answer: Anand saw himself as a scientist and enjoyed tinkering with electrical gadgets, so he designed a detailed alarm to help the colony after many thefts. However, his inventions usually did not work as intended. His belief in his own ability therefore did not guarantee that the burglar alarm would succeed.
points: Identifies Anand’s belief that he was a scientist
Links his interest in gadgets to the alarm design
Explains his motivation after the recent thefts
Notes that his inventions usually missed their intended result
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A burglar opened the door gently, and the alarm rang loudly. A water bag fell on the burglar’s head. Anand planned to call the police, but Anita doubted that the alarm could identify a burglar. She asked Anand to clean the mess before anyone returned. Anand tried no new invention for a week. Then the family watched ‘Back to the Future’, about a time machine. The film ended the peace and quiet, and Anand decided to make a time machine too.
activities.prompt: If the door were opened roughly instead of gently, what would most likely happen?
options: The warning system would remain silent.
The alarm would ring at once.
The water bag would drop as usual.
The alarm would ring more softly.

A rough opening would not meet the alarm’s condition.
The water bag falls after the alarm sounds.
The alarm was designed to make a loud sound, not a softer one.

activities.explanation: The alarm works only when the door is opened gently.

activities.context: A burglar opened the door gently, and the alarm rang loudly. A water bag fell on the burglar’s head. Anand planned to call the police, but Anita doubted that the alarm could identify a burglar. She asked Anand to clean the mess before anyone returned. Anand tried no new invention for a week. Then the family watched ‘Back to the Future’, about a time machine. The film ended the peace and quiet, and Anand decided to make a time machine too.
activities.prompt: Why did Anita doubt that the alarm could identify a burglar?
options: It could not tell one opener from another.
It would only sound after a gentle opening.
The water bag was too light to notice.
It could ring even when no one entered.

why.It would only sound after a gentle openi: The gentle-opening condition explains when it sounds, not who triggered it.
Nothing in the case suggests that the water bag was too light.
Whether it sounds without someone entering does not explain identification.

activities.explanation: The alarm could show that the door was opened, but not who opened it.

activities.prompt: Explain why the alarm might fail to protect the family completely.
activities.answer: The alarm was rigged to work only when the door was opened gently. If it was opened another way, the alarm might not ring, and the water bag would not fall because it falls after the alarm sounds. Anita also doubted that the sounding alarm could identify the burglar.
points: The alarm needs a gentle opening to work.
A rough opening might prevent the alarm from sounding.
The water bag falls only after the alarm sounds.
The alarm might not identify who opened the door.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why Anand should keep his promise after Papa refuses permission and Ma worries about the children being alone.
activities.answer: Anand should keep his promise because Papa has firmly refused permission, and Ma is worried about the children being alone. Waiting until his parents return shows that Anand respects their decisions and does not use the time machine while they are not there.
points: Papa refused permission
Ma worried about the children being alone
Anand promised to wait
Breaking the promise would be wrong
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Late one night, Anita heard scratching, a rattle and a click. She woke Anand and said someone was outside. Anita recognised the intruder as Boppa, who had begun searching the compounds in their row. She realised that Boppa was the thief. He threatened them to remain quiet and waved his cudgel as he backed out. Anand tricked him into entering his own room instead of Papa’s. A crash and loud scream came from there. Then neighbours ran up the drive.
activities.prompt: What was Anand’s most likely reason for tricking Boppa into entering his own room instead of Papa’s room?
options: To keep Boppa away from Papa’s room.
To show Boppa that Anand was not afraid of him.
To help Boppa find what he was searching for.
To make Boppa trust Anand completely.

why.To show Boppa that Anand was not afraid: Bravado does not explain Anand’s practical choice.
why.To help Boppa find what he was searching: Helping the intruder would not protect the family.
Gaining trust was not suggested by what happened.

activities.explanation: The trick redirected the intruder away from Papa’s room.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between recognising the intruder and realising that he was the thief?
activities.answer: Recognising the intruder means Anita knew that the person outside was Boppa. Realising that he was the thief means she also understood his purpose in searching the compounds in their row. One was about identity; the other was about his criminal role.
points: Recognition identifies the person as Boppa
Understanding his role explains his purpose
The search of the compounds provides the connection
Clearly separates identity from criminal role
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Sharma Uncle and the other neighbours unlocked Anand’s door and entered his room cautiously. After they turned on the lights, they noticed that the time machine was humming softly. They checked how Boppa could leave the house and found his green scarf near the switches. They searched everywhere in case he was still there, but he could not be found. Boppa was never seen again.
activities.prompt: After finding Boppa’s scarf near the switches but not seeing Boppa, what is the best next step?
options: Check whether Boppa might still be inside and search the house.
Put the scarf away and leave without checking further.
Ask the neighbours to wait outside while the lights remain on.
Treat the humming machine as proof that Boppa is nearby.

why.Put the scarf away and leave without che: The scarf alone does not show whether Boppa remains in the house.
why.Ask the neighbours to wait outside while: The search would be incomplete if they stopped before checking inside.
why.Treat the humming machine as proof that: The machine humming does not prove that Boppa is nearby.

activities.explanation: This checks whether Boppa is still inside before anyone concludes that he is gone.

activities.context: Sharma Uncle and the other neighbours unlocked Anand’s door and entered his room cautiously. After they turned on the lights, they noticed that the time machine was humming softly. They checked how Boppa could leave the house and found his green scarf near the switches. They searched everywhere in case he was still there, but he could not be found. Boppa was never seen again.
activities.prompt: After Boppa was never seen again, what does Anand’s continued belief show about how he understands the events?
options: He accepts that the machine worked even though Boppa was not found.
He thinks the search proves that Boppa left in an ordinary way.
He believes the scarf shows that the lights caused Boppa to disappear.
He accepts that the machine failed because Boppa was never found.

why.He thinks the search proves that Boppa l: The facts do not establish an ordinary way for Boppa to leave.
why.He believes the scarf shows that the lig: The scarf’s position does not explain Boppa’s disappearance.
why.He accepts that the machine failed becau: Boppa’s absence did not make Anand accept that the machine failed.

activities.explanation: This correctly describes Anand’s continued belief.

activities.prompt: How did the neighbours respond after opening Anand’s room, and what did their search show?
activities.answer: The neighbours unlocked the door and entered Anand’s room cautiously. They turned on the lights and noticed the softly humming time machine. They found Boppa’s green scarf near the switches, checked how he could leave, and searched the house. However, they could not find him anywhere.
points: They unlocked the door and entered cautiously.
They turned on the lights and heard the machine humming.
They found the scarf and searched the house.
Boppa could not be found anywhere.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a lesson, ISRO launched the satellite Rohini into near-Earth orbit. Dr Narinder Singh Kapany played an important part in inventing fibre optics. Students were asked to distinguish these achievements in terms of creativity, innovation, and invention. In a classroom example, Anand was described as creative and experimental, while Anita showed responsibility by asking Anand to clean up the mess. The lesson also reviewed onomatopoeia, binomials, and idioms.
activities.prompt: ISRO launched Rohini into near-Earth orbit. Which label best explains this action?
options: Innovation, because the organisation did something new.
Creativity, because the organisation thought of a new thing.
An idiom, because the action meant more than the words literally.
A binomial, because the action joined two linked words.

why.Creativity, because the organisation tho: This confuses thinking new things with actually doing them.
why.An idiom, because the action meant more: An idiom concerns meaning that is different from literal meaning.
why.A binomial, because the action joined tw: A binomial is an expression made from two linked words.

activities.explanation: This matches innovation, which means doing new things.

activities.context: During a lesson, ISRO launched the satellite Rohini into near-Earth orbit. Dr Narinder Singh Kapany played an important part in inventing fibre optics. Students were asked to distinguish these achievements in terms of creativity, innovation, and invention. In a classroom example, Anand was described as creative and experimental, while Anita showed responsibility by asking Anand to clean up the mess. The lesson also reviewed onomatopoeia, binomials, and idioms.
activities.prompt: Why does Anita's request to have the mess cleaned show responsibility?
options: She is taking responsibility for making sure the mess is dealt with.
She is inventing a new way to describe the mess.
She is thinking of new onomatopoeic words for the mess.
She is showing that the mess is a binomial expression.

why.She is inventing a new way to describe t: Describing the mess does not show responsibility for dealing with it.
why.She is thinking of new onomatopoeic word: Creating sound-imitating words is about language, not responsibility.
why.She is showing that the mess is a binomi: Identifying an expression as a binomial does not explain the request.

activities.explanation: Asking Anand to clean up makes sure the mess does not remain.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between creativity, innovation, and invention.
activities.answer: Creativity means thinking new things, whereas innovation means doing new things. An invention brings ideas or objects together in a novel way to create something new. Dr Kapany's fibre optics work illustrates invention, while ISRO's launch of Rohini illustrates innovation.
points: Creativity means thinking new things.
Innovation means doing new things.
An invention brings ideas or objects together in a novel way to create something new.
The examples distinguish the three ideas.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

are expressions made from two linked words

chapters.title: The Tunnel
chapters.summary: In this chapter: waiting beside the cutting; exploring the dark tunnel; meeting sunder singh; an evening in the jungle.

lessons.title: Waiting Beside the Cutting

activities.prompt: What was Suraj waiting for beside the cutting that day?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Midday Train
activities.body: It was almost noon, and the jungle was very still. Suraj stood near the cutting and waited for the midday train. He was not at a station and was not catching a train. He left his cycle at a village and walked to the tunnel exit. He heard a shrill whistle, then a sound like distant thunder. The steam engine came out, and he stepped back from the hot steam.
keyPoints: The jungle was still at almost noon.
Suraj waited near the cutting, not at a station.
He heard a whistle and a thunder-like sound before the engine came out.
activities.explanation: This story moves from a silent wait to a loud train arrival.

activities.prompt: Why did Suraj step back when the engine came out?
steps: The engine shot out of the tunnel.
Hot steam then struck Suraj’s face.
He stepped back to keep the hot steam away from his face.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where was Suraj waiting?
options: At the village
Near the cutting
At a station
Inside the tunnel
activities.explanation: Suraj stood near the cutting while he waited for the midday train.

activities.prompt: Suraj was waiting to catch the midday train.
activities.explanation: He was waiting for the train, but he was not catching it.

activities.prompt: How did Suraj reach the tunnel exit?
options: He cycled there
He rode there by train
He walked there
He was carried there
activities.explanation: He left his cycle at the village, then walked to the tunnel exit.

activities.prompt: The engine’s shrill ______ sounded in the distance.
activities.hint: It was the engine’s sharp sound.
activities.explanation: The engine’s shrill whistle sounded in the distance.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with its matching detail.
activities.explanation: Each clue points to a sound, feeling, or sight in the story.

activities.prompt: Why could Suraj not see the train?
options: Smoke covered the train near the tunnel.
Shisham trees stood between him and it.
The train was hidden deep inside the tunnel.
The train was beyond the hill’s other side.
activities.explanation: The train was approaching from the other side of the hill.

activities.prompt: The plume of smoke stayed inside the tunnel.
activities.explanation: Instead, it drifted lazily over the tall shisham trees.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order Suraj experienced them.
items: He left his cycle at a village.
He heard the engine’s shrill whistle.
He heard a sound like distant thunder.
The steam engine shot out of the tunnel.
He stepped back from the hot steam.
activities.explanation: The whistle came first, then the tunnel sound, the engine, and Suraj stepping back.

activities.prompt: The jungle was very still at almost noon. What does this suggest?
options: A loud sound would stand out in the silence.
The jungle was already crowded with activity.
Far-off sounds could not be heard at all.
Hot steam had already filled the trees.

why.The jungle was already crowded with acti: The silence shows the opposite of crowding.
why.Far-off sounds could not be heard at all: A distant whistle is later heard, so sounds can be heard.
Steam appears later, and it does not explain the silence.

activities.explanation: The silence explains why the shrill whistle stood out.

activities.prompt: Hot steam strikes your face beside a railway cutting. What should you do?
options: Step back before the steam reaches you.
Move closer so you can see better.
Stay still and wait for the steam.
Wave both hands beside the steam.

Moving closer would bring you nearer the hot steam.
Waiting would leave your face in the steam.
Waving does not stop hot steam from striking you.

activities.explanation: Suraj stepped back because the steam was hot.

lessons.title: Exploring the Dark Tunnel

activities.prompt: What would Suraj discover as he ventured deeper inside the tunnel?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Walk Through the Tunnel
activities.body: Suraj walked into a tunnel to learn what it was like. As he walked farther, the tunnel grew darker. Twenty yards inside, it was completely dark. The walls were damp and sticky. A bat flew past, and a lizard moved between the railway lines. The watchman inspected and cleared obstacles. Obstacles are things that block the path. He used a red flag to warn the driver of danger.
keyPoints: The tunnel became darker as Suraj walked farther inside.
The tunnel was completely dark twenty yards inside.
The watchman inspected the tunnel and cleared obstacles.
activities.explanation: This lesson follows Suraj's walk and the watchman's work.

activities.prompt: What would Suraj experience inside a dark tunnel?
steps: He walked deeper to know what a tunnel was really like.
It became completely dark about twenty yards inside.
He could still see the other opening as a small circle of light.
Damp walls and moving animals made the tunnel feel real.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happened as Suraj walked farther into the tunnel?
options: It became darker.
It became brighter.
It stayed the same.
It became warmer.
activities.explanation: The tunnel became darker as Suraj walked farther into it. You followed the change in light.

activities.prompt: He could see the other ______ as a small circle of light.
activities.hint: Look at the word for the way out.
activities.explanation: The other opening appeared as a small circle of light.

activities.prompt: Why did Suraj walk through the tunnel?
options: To know what tunnels are really like.
To find the far opening.
To watch a train pass.
To meet the watchman.
activities.explanation: Suraj walked through so he would know what a tunnel was really like.

activities.prompt: What was the watchman's duty?
options: Inspect tunnels and clear obstacles.
Guide the driver through tunnels.
Watch the railway lines for lizards.
Carry a red flag into tunnels.
activities.explanation: His duty was to inspect the tunnel and clear it of obstacles.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it did or meant.
pairs: Inspected the tunnel and cleared obstacles
activities.explanation: Each pair matches an action or duty from the tunnel story.

activities.prompt: Put Suraj's walk in order.
items: Suraj walks farther into the tunnel
The tunnel becomes darker
It becomes completely dark
activities.explanation: As Suraj walks farther, the tunnel grows darker and then becomes completely dark.

activities.prompt: The tunnel became darker as Suraj walked further into it. How might he have felt?
options: He may have felt nervous because the light was fading.
He may have felt excited because the tunnel was darker.
He may have felt relieved because the tunnel was darker.
He may have felt bored because the tunnel was darker.

why.He may have felt excited because the tun: Feeling excited treats greater darkness as something enjoyable.
why.He may have felt relieved because the tu: Feeling relieved treats greater darkness as comforting.
why.He may have felt bored because the tunne: Feeling bored treats the changing tunnel as uninteresting.

activities.explanation: Feeling nervous fits because the tunnel kept becoming darker.

activities.prompt: A lizard scuttled between the railway lines. What does “scuttled” suggest about its movement?
options: It moved quickly and lightly between the lines.
It moved slowly and carefully between the lines.
It stayed still between the lines.
It moved high above the railway lines.

why.It moved slowly and carefully between th: Scuttled is wrongly understood as slow, careful movement.
Staying still ignores the movement shown by the word.
Above the lines changes the place given in the sentence.

activities.explanation: Scuttled suggests quick, light movement between the lines.

activities.prompt: The tunnel became darker. Its walls were damp and sticky, and a bat flew past. A lizard scuttled between the railway lines. What do these details suggest?
options: They make the tunnel feel real and somewhat unsettling.
They make the tunnel feel bright and welcoming.
They show that no living things were near Suraj.
They show that the tunnel had no difficult parts.

why.They make the tunnel feel bright and wel: Bright and welcoming does not match the dark, damp surroundings.
why.They show that no living things were nea: No living things is wrong because a bat and lizard appear.
why.They show that the tunnel had no difficu: No difficult parts ignores the damp, sticky tunnel walls.

activities.explanation: Damp walls and moving animals make the tunnel feel real and unsettling.

lessons.title: Meeting Sunder Singh

activities.prompt: What surprises might await Suraj during his afternoon adventure?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meeting at the Tunnel
activities.body: Suraj appears while a watchman is taking an afternoon nap. The watchman welcomes Suraj and asks why he is inspecting the tunnel. The watchman had lent the tunnel to the Government. Suraj wanted to watch the train and then walk through the tunnel. He thought he saw an animal on the hill. The watchman called it his leopard.
keyPoints: The watchman was taking an afternoon nap.
Suraj wanted to watch the train and walk through the tunnel.
The animal was the watchman's leopard.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the meeting and the important details.

activities.prompt: Why did Suraj look toward the hill while he was near the tunnel?
steps: He wanted to watch the train and walk through the tunnel, because he was inspecting the area.
He saw an animal moving on the hill, because its movement caught his attention.
The watchman said it was his leopard, because he knew the animal.
So Suraj looked toward the hill because he thought an animal was there.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What was the watchman doing when Suraj appeared?
options: Taking an afternoon nap
Walking through the tunnel
Watching the train
Inspecting the hill
activities.explanation: The watchman was taking an afternoon nap when Suraj appeared.

activities.prompt: The watchman said that the animal was his ______.
activities.hint: This animal came to the range for a few days every month.
activities.explanation: He called it his leopard. It came to the range for a few days every month.

activities.prompt: What did Suraj want to do?
options: Watch the train and walk through the tunnel
Watch the leopard and inspect the hill
Walk through the jungle and watch the train
Inspect the tunnel and meet the train
activities.explanation: Suraj wanted to watch the train and then walk through the tunnel.

activities.prompt: Match each person or animal with what the lesson says.
pairs: Came to the range every month
activities.explanation: The leopard came for a few days every month. Sunder Singh had lived there for many years.

activities.prompt: Put the events in the order they happen in the lesson.
items: Suraj appeared while the watchman napped
The watchman welcomed Suraj
The watchman asked why Suraj was inspecting
The watchman said he had lent the tunnel
activities.explanation: The watchman was napping when Suraj appeared. He then welcomed and questioned Suraj.

activities.prompt: Which summary matches what Sunder Singh said?
options: Lived there for many years; jungle safer
Visited there for a few days; town safer
Lived there for many years; town safer
Visited there for many years; jungle safer
activities.explanation: He had lived there for many years. The jungle was safer than the town.

activities.prompt: Suraj appears while the watchman is taking an afternoon nap. How does the watchman most likely feel?
options: He seems surprised, but willing to talk.
He seems angry that Suraj woke him.
He seems calm because he knows Suraj.
He seems afraid because Suraj is close.

This mistake thinks waking him automatically made him angry.
Knowing Suraj is not shown by the facts.
Being close does not show that the watchman feared Suraj.

activities.explanation: Welcoming Suraj shows that the watchman is friendly and willing to talk.

activities.prompt: The watchman asks why Suraj is inspecting the tunnel. He then says that he lent it to the Government. What does his statement do?
options: It gives a reason for his presence there.
It gives Suraj permission to enter.
It describes how fast the train moves.
It explains when the leopard visits.

This mistake confuses an explanation with permission.
Nothing in the statement describes the train's speed.
The leopard is a separate matter from the Government and the tunnel.

activities.explanation: The Government detail explains why the watchman is staying near the tunnel.

activities.prompt: The watchman says his leopard comes to the range for a few days each month. What can Suraj expect?
options: The leopard may return in another month.
The leopard may never return again.
The leopard may stay there all year.
The leopard may follow every train.

This mistake ignores the regular monthly visits.
Staying for only a few days does not mean staying all year.
Nothing connects the leopard's visits with following trains.

activities.explanation: A monthly visit means the leopard may come back the next month.

activities.prompt: Railway tracks go through a hill, and Suraj plans to walk that way. What does “tunnel” mean here?
options: A passage going through the hill.
A path going over the hill.
A train that runs through hills.
A room built inside the hill.

Going over the hill describes a path, not a tunnel.
This mistake names the train instead of the passage.
A room is a building, not a railway passage.

activities.explanation: A tunnel is a passage that goes through the hill.

activities.prompt: Sunder Singh has lived in the jungle for many years. He says the jungle is safer than the town. What does this suggest about him?
options: He knows the jungle well and trusts it.
He has never visited the town.
He wants Suraj to leave the jungle.
He thinks all animals are harmless.

Living in the jungle does not prove that he never visited the town.
His belief about safety does not show that he wanted Suraj to leave.
Trusting the jungle does not mean thinking every animal is harmless.

activities.explanation: His long stay and safety belief suggest knowledge and trust in the jungle.

lessons.title: An Evening in the Jungle

activities.prompt: What might Suraj and the watchman discover in the tunnel?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sounds After Sunset
activities.body: Suraj returns to the watchman's hut on the following evening. The earth cools as a light breeze carries the scent of mango blossoms. Suraj and Sunder Singh drink tea and listen to birds. At twilight, the birds fall silent. Sunder Singh lights his oil lamp and goes to inspect the tunnel. A footfall and rustling leaves make the watchman stop. A sawing sound makes them think the leopard is inside.
keyPoints: The breeze carries the scent of mango blossoms.
The birds fall silent as twilight fades.
New sounds make the watchman stop.
activities.explanation: The evening moves from tea and birds to quiet, strange sounds.

activities.prompt: Why did the watchman stop when sounds came near the forest tunnel?
steps: He heard a footfall and a rustle of leaves.
He stopped because the sounds showed something had moved nearby.
A sawing sound then made them think a leopard was inside.
So stopping and listening helped them check for danger.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Listening in the Dark
activities.body: After the birds fall silent, Sunder Singh lights his oil lamp. He goes to inspect the tunnel. Suraj hears a barking deer, a fox and a nightjar in the forest. Then a footfall and a rustle of leaves make the watchman stop. Next, a sawing sound makes them think the leopard is inside.
keyPoints: The oil lamp is lit after the birds fall silent.
The watchman stops after hearing a footfall and rustling leaves.
A sawing sound makes them think of a leopard.
activities.explanation: Each sound changes what Suraj and the watchman think.

activities.prompt: What did the breeze carry through the trees?
options: mango blossom scent
watchman footfalls
nightjar calls
barking deer calls
activities.explanation: The breeze carried the scent of mango blossoms.

activities.prompt: Suraj and Sunder Singh drank tea while listening to ______.
activities.hint: They could hear them around them.
activities.explanation: They listened to birds while they drank tea.

activities.prompt: Match each subject with the change or action described in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a change or action described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Why did the watchman stop?
options: He heard a footfall and rustling.
He heard birds and nightjar calls.
He smelled mango blossom scent.
He watched twilight fading.
activities.explanation: The watchman stopped after hearing a footfall and rustling leaves.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen in the lesson.
items: The birds fell silent.
Sunder Singh lit his oil lamp.
Sunder Singh went to inspect the tunnel.
Suraj heard a barking deer, a fox and a nightjar.
A footfall and rustling leaves made the watchman stop.
activities.explanation: The items follow the sequence of events in the lesson.

activities.prompt: What did the sawing sound make them think?
options: The leopard was inside the tunnel.
The fox was inside the tunnel.
The deer was inside the tunnel.
The nightjar was inside the tunnel.
activities.explanation: The sawing sound made them think the leopard was inside.

activities.prompt: The watchman watered his garden and boiled water for tea. Suraj and Sunder Singh drank tea while listening to birds. How does this scene make the evening feel?
options: Quiet and peaceful.
Loud and hurried.
Cold and empty.
Bright and busy.

The garden work and shared tea show a slow evening, not a hurried one.
Boiling water and drinking tea do not make the evening feel cold.
Bird sounds and shared tea suggest a quiet moment, not a busy one.

activities.explanation: Drinking tea and listening to birds suggest a calm and peaceful evening.

activities.prompt: A light breeze carried the scent of mango blossoms through the trees. What does the breeze suggest about the weather?
options: Rain may come soon.
Rain will never come.
Hot weather will continue.
Strong wind will begin.

A promise of rain means rain is possible, not impossible.
The breeze was moving and the earth was cooling, not staying hot.
The breeze was light, so it did not signal strong wind.

activities.explanation: The breeze promised rain, so rain may come soon.

activities.prompt: After twilight faded, Suraj heard three animals in the forest. What does this show about the forest?
options: Several animals were awake around him.
Only the watchman was outside.
All the animals were asleep.
The forest had no night sounds.

Suraj heard three animals, so more than one living thing was active.
Their calls show that the animals were awake, not asleep.
Suraj heard three animals, so the forest still had sounds.

activities.explanation: The three different animal sounds show that animals were awake.

activities.prompt: A footfall and a rustle of leaves made the watchman stop. What was he most likely trying to find out?
options: Where the nearby sounds came from.
When the birds would sing again.
Why the garden needed water.
When the rain would arrive.

The birds had fallen silent, so their return was not the reason.
He had already watered the garden, so water was not the issue.
The breeze promised rain, but these sounds did not give its time.

activities.explanation: The sounds made him stop, so he was checking their source.

activities.prompt: A sawing sound made both men think a leopard was inside. How did this affect their feelings?
options: It made them alert and cautious.
It made them relaxed and carefree.
It made them return to the tea.
It made them forget the sounds.

They had shared tea, but the possible leopard changed the mood.
They thought the sawing sound came from making tea.
A worrying sound would not make them forget it.

activities.explanation: Thinking a leopard was inside made them alert and cautious.

lessons.title: Driving the Leopard Away

activities.prompt: What would you do if a leopard blocked your path?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Leopard in the Tunnel
activities.body: Sunder Singh entered the tunnel with his lamp and shouted. Suraj followed, but his dry throat stopped him shouting. They saw a leopard crouching between the tracks, only five metres away. It bared its teeth and snarled. Suraj and Sunder Singh shouted together. Their voices rang through the tunnel. The leopard turned swiftly and disappeared into the darkness. They walked the whole tunnel to make sure it had gone.
keyPoints: Sunder Singh entered the tunnel first with his lamp.
Suraj followed, but his dry throat stopped him shouting.
Their loud voices made the leopard disappear.
activities.explanation: The pair faced the leopard together, then checked the tunnel.

activities.prompt: How can the boys make the leopard leave?
steps: The leopard is close and snarls, so the boys face danger.
Sunder Singh shouts, but Suraj cannot because his throat is dry.
Suraj also shouts, and their voices ring through the tunnel.
The leopard disappears, so their shouting seems to work.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Entered First?
activities.prompt: Who entered the tunnel with a lamp and shouted?
options: Suraj
The leopard
Sunder Singh
The train
activities.explanation: Sunder Singh entered first, carrying his lamp and shouting.

activities.title: How Far Away?
activities.prompt: The leopard was only ______ metres away from them.
activities.hint: Think of the distance given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The leopard was only five metres away from Suraj and Sunder Singh.

activities.title: Match the Details
activities.prompt: Match each beginning with its matching ending.
activities.explanation: Each detail matches the correct person, place, object, or movement.

activities.title: Into the Darkness
activities.prompt: What happened after their voices rang through the tunnel?
options: It turned and disappeared into the darkness.
It crouched between the tracks.
It began to hum like the rails.
It entered the tunnel again.
activities.explanation: The leopard turned swiftly and disappeared into the darkness.

activities.title: Events in Order
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Sunder Singh entered with his lamp.
Suraj followed behind him.
They saw the leopard between the tracks.
They shouted together.
The leopard disappeared.
activities.explanation: The story moves from entering the tunnel to the leopard's disappearance.

activities.title: Checking the Tunnel
activities.prompt: Why did they walk the whole tunnel after the leopard disappeared?
options: To confirm the leopard had gone.
To view the train from the rails.
To hear Suraj shout once more.
To watch the rails stop humming.
activities.explanation: They walked the whole tunnel to make sure the leopard had gone.

activities.prompt: Suraj cannot shout because his throat is dry. What does this show?
options: He wants to shout, but his throat cannot yet.
He is careless and does not want to help.
He is angry with Sunder Singh for shouting.
He has left the tunnel and gone far away.

why.He is careless and does not want to help: This mistakes physical trouble for a lack of care.
why.He is angry with Sunder Singh for shouti: Nothing shows that Suraj is angry with Sunder Singh.
why.He has left the tunnel and gone far away: Suraj follows behind, so he has not left the tunnel.

activities.explanation: His dry throat explains why he cannot shout at first.

activities.prompt: The leopard is five metres away and snarls. What does this mean?
options: The leopard is close and may attack the boys.
The leopard is far away and cannot see them.
The leopard is friendly and plans to sleep.
The leopard is weak and cannot hurt the boys.

why.The leopard is far away and cannot see t: This ignores both the short distance and the threatening teeth.
why.The leopard is friendly and plans to sle: Baring teeth and snarling show threat, not friendliness.
why.The leopard is weak and cannot hurt the: The leopard looks strong, not weak and harmless.

activities.explanation: Five metres is close, and baring teeth shows danger.

activities.prompt: The leopard is not very big. What do lithe and sinewy suggest?
options: It is slim and has a strong, flexible body.
It is huge and heavy, with very strong muscles.
It is weak and cannot move its body at all.
It is soft and round, with short and thick legs.

why.It is huge and heavy, with very strong m: This treats a small leopard as if it were huge and heavy.
why.It is weak and cannot move its body at a: Sinewy suggests strength, not an inability to move.
why.It is soft and round, with short and thi: These words suggest a slim, strong body, not a soft one.

activities.explanation: Lithe means flexible, and sinewy means strong and thin.

activities.prompt: Their voices ring through the tunnel. Why does the leopard leave?
options: The loud voices frightened the leopard away.
The approaching train frightened the leopard away.
The lamp made the leopard leave the tunnel.
The leopard was tired and wanted to sleep.

why.The approaching train frightened the leo: The train only approaches after the leopard has disappeared.
why.The lamp made the leopard leave the tunn: The lamp helps them, but it does not explain the leopard's exit.
why.The leopard was tired and wanted to slee: Nothing shows that the leopard was tired or wanted to sleep.

activities.explanation: The leopard turns and disappears just after their loud voices.

lessons.title: The Journey a Week Later

activities.prompt: What surprises awaited Suraj during his mysterious train journey?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Night Train Journey
activities.body: About a week later, Suraj travelled in the same train as his father. His father was travelling to Delhi on a business trip. The night mail carried hundreds of passengers through the forest. Suraj sat by an open window and looked into the darkness. He could not see Sunder Singh, but he knew his friend was there.
keyPoints: Suraj shared the train with his father about a week later.
The night mail went through the forest.
Suraj knew Sunder Singh was nearby without seeing him.
activities.explanation: These details show the people, place and mood during the journey.

activities.prompt: Why might Suraj feel lonely even though Sunder Singh is on the same train?
steps: Suraj looks into the darkness, so he cannot clearly see his surroundings.
He cannot see Sunder Singh, so his friend seems absent from view.
He knows his friend is there, so he is not truly alone.
Therefore, Suraj may feel lonely without thinking his friend has left.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Suraj's Place
activities.prompt: Where did Suraj sit during the journey?
options: By an open window
Beside a closed door
Under a train bench
Near the engine
activities.explanation: This detail shows where Suraj sat during the night journey.

activities.title: The Business Trip
activities.prompt: His father was travelling to ______ on a business trip.
activities.hint: This city was the father's destination.
activities.explanation: His father was going to Delhi for business.

activities.prompt: Suraj travelled in the same train with his father about a week later.
activities.explanation: This matches the time and the shared train in the lesson.

activities.title: Journey Details
activities.prompt: Match each part of the journey with its detail.
pairs: He wrote in a notebook while doing his accounts
It carried hundreds of passengers through the forest
They flickered past the small villages
They kept a steady rhythm on the rails
It made him seem like a firefly
activities.explanation: Each detail helps you picture the busy and mysterious night journey.

activities.prompt: The carriage wheels stopped their steady rhythm on the rails.
activities.explanation: The wheels kept a steady rhythm, so the train had a steady sound.

activities.title: Leaving the Jungle
activities.prompt: What happened when the train went through the tunnel?
options: It left the jungle behind
It entered another village
It stopped for the night
It lost its steady rhythm
activities.explanation: After the tunnel, the train left the jungle behind.

The notebook and accounts are far apart.

activities.context: It was almost noon, and the jungle was still. Suraj waited near the cutting for the midday train, though he was not catching it. activities.prompt: Why could Suraj not see the train when he first heard the whistle?
options: The hill hid the approaching engine from Suraj’s view.
The whistle was so faint that it could only be mistaken for another sound.
The train was still inside the tunnel, where no one could see it.
The trees were blocking every view of the line.

why.The whistle was so faint that it could o: A shrill whistle was clearly audible.
why.The train was still inside the tunnel, w: The train was approaching the tunnel, not waiting inside it.
why.The trees were blocking every view of th: The trees were above the smoke, not blocking the whole view.

activities.explanation: The train was approaching from the hill’s other side.

activities.context: It was almost noon, and the jungle was still. Suraj waited near the cutting for the midday train, though he was not catching it. The train will stop beside the cutting so Suraj can board it.
The engine will pass behind the hill and vanish without entering the tunnel.
Suraj will hear no further sound because the jungle remains silent.

why.The engine will pass behind the hill and: Suraj was not at a station or catching the train.
why.Suraj will hear no further sound because: The sounds showed that the train was approaching.

activities.explanation: The engine emerged immediately after the sound.

activities.prompt: Explain why Suraj could hear the train before he could see it.
activities.answer: Suraj heard the engine’s shrill whistle while the train was approaching from the other side of the hill. The hill blocked his view, so the sound reached him first. Soon afterward, the thunder-like noise came from the tunnel, and the engine emerged.
points: The engine’s shrill whistle was heard in the distance.
The train was approaching from the other side of the hill.
The hill blocked Suraj’s view of the train.
The engine later emerged from the tunnel.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Suraj entered the tunnel because he wanted to know what a tunnel was really like. As he walked farther inside, it became darker, and about twenty yards in, it was completely dark. He could see the other opening as a small circle of light. Damp, sticky walls surrounded him, a bat flew past, and a lizard scuttled between the railway lines. The watchman inspected the tunnel and cleared obstacles, using a red flag to warn the driver about danger.
activities.prompt: If Suraj had moved only a little way inside, how would the tunnel probably look?
options: It would be darker than at the entrance, but not totally dark.
It would already be completely dark, with no light visible.
It would remain exactly as bright as it was at the entrance.
It would be so dark that the other opening could not be seen.

why.It would already be completely dark, wit: Complete darkness occurred only about twenty yards inside.
why.It would remain exactly as bright as it: The darkness increased rather than remaining unchanged.
why.It would be so dark that the other openi: Even in complete darkness, the other opening could still be seen as light.

activities.explanation: The tunnel became darker as Suraj walked farther inside.

activities.context: Suraj entered the tunnel because he wanted to know what a tunnel was really like. As he walked farther inside, it became darker, and about twenty yards in, it was completely dark. He could see the other opening as a small circle of light. Damp, sticky walls surrounded him, a bat flew past, and a lizard scuttled between the railway lines. The watchman inspected the tunnel and cleared obstacles, using a red flag to warn the driver about danger.
activities.prompt: If the watchman finds an obstacle between the railway lines, what is his duty?

Leave it there because noticing it is enough.
Ask Suraj to clear it before continuing.
Use the red flag but leave the obstacle in place.

why.Leave it there because noticing it is en: His duty is to remove obstacles, not merely notice them.
Suraj is exploring and is not responsible for the watchman's duty.
why.Use the red flag but leave the obstacle: Warning the driver does not replace clearing the obstacle.

activities.prompt: Explain how the tunnel's appearance and atmosphere changed as Suraj walked farther inside.

points: The tunnel became darker as Suraj walked farther inside.
It became completely dark about twenty yards inside.
The other opening remained visible as a small circle of light.
The damp walls, bat, and lizard affected the atmosphere.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Suraj arrived while the watchman, Sunder Singh, took an afternoon nap. He was welcomed and asked why he was inspecting the tunnel. He wanted to watch the train and walk through, but had seen an animal on the hill. Sunder Singh said it was his leopard, which visited the range for a few days every month. activities.prompt: Suraj still wants to walk through the tunnel after seeing the animal. What should he do next?
options: Ask Sunder Singh about the animal before going through.
Enter at once because the tunnel had been lent to the Government.
Follow the leopard into the range immediately.
Wait until the night mail arrives and then enter without asking.

why.Enter at once because the tunnel had bee: The Government loan does not tell Suraj what to do about the animal.
why.Follow the leopard into the range immedi: The leopard is in the range, so following it would ignore the risk.
why.Wait until the night mail arrives and th: The night mail's arrival does not answer Suraj's question about the animal.

activities.explanation: Correct: Suraj needs the watchman's explanation before entering.

activities.context: Suraj arrived while the watchman, Sunder Singh, took an afternoon nap. He was welcomed and asked why he was inspecting the tunnel. activities.prompt: Suppose the daytime train did not run on a particular day. Which arrival could still take place?

The daytime train could arrive around nine instead.
The night mail could arrive during the afternoon.
The daytime train could arrive twice, once by day and once around nine.

why.The daytime train could arrive around ni: The daytime train was the service that ran by day.
why.The night mail could arrive during the a: The night mail's stated arrival time was about nine.
why.The daytime train could arrive twice, on: Only one train ran by day, so a second arrival is not supported.

activities.prompt: How do Suraj's purpose and Sunder Singh's question about the inspection relate to one another?

He also planned to walk through the tunnel.
The watchman welcomed Suraj.
The watchman asked why Suraj was inspecting the tunnel.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: How did the sounds in the forest change as evening went on?
activities.answer: At first, Suraj and Sunder Singh listened to birds while drinking tea. When twilight disappeared, the birds became quiet. Later, Suraj heard a barking deer, a fox and a nightjar. Thus, the forest moved from birdsong to silence and then to sounds made by three animals.
points: Birds were heard during tea.
The birds became quiet when twilight disappeared.
Suraj later heard a barking deer, a fox and a nightjar.
The sound changed from birdsong to silence and animal sounds.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a tunnel, Sunder Singh entered with his lamp and shouted. Suraj followed, but his throat was dry. They saw a leopard crouching between the tracks, five metres away. It bared its teeth and snarled as it lowered its body. Suraj and Sunder Singh shouted together. Their voices rang through the tunnel, and the leopard turned swiftly and disappeared into the darkness. activities.prompt: Which explanation best tells us why Suraj did not shout when he first entered the tunnel?

Dryness in his throat prevented him from calling out.
He thought the lamp would make his shout unnecessary.
He was too far from the tunnel entrance for his voice to carry.

why.He had not yet seen the leopard when he: He had already seen the leopard.
why.He thought the lamp would make his shout: The lamp did not replace the need to call out.
why.He was too far from the tunnel entrance: Suraj was close enough to join the later shout.

activities.explanation: His dry throat explains his silence.

This explains why he could not shout initially.

Their voices rang through the tunnel.

lessons.title: The National War Memorial: A Place of Remembrance

activities.prompt: Why do we visit the National War Memorial to remember our brave soldiers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Remembering the Cost of Freedom
activities.body: India had to fight several wars to protect its borders. The National War Memorial was built between April 2018 and February 2019. It covers more than 40 acres near India Gate. The memorial pays tribute to some of the bravest Indians and remembers the heavy cost of winning freedom. Its tablets carry the names of soldiers who fought for India.
keyPoints: The memorial remembers India's wars and brave soldiers.
Each tablet carries a soldier's name.
Freedom and security depend on brave sacrifices.
activities.explanation: A memorial helps us remember brave service members and the cost of freedom.

activities.prompt: At a school visit near India Gate, a child sees many tablets. Why should the child remember the soldiers?
steps: Each tablet records a soldier's service because it carries that soldier's name.
This matters because freedom and security depend on brave service members.
The child stands quietly because remembrance keeps those sacrifices in memory.
So the child should honour the soldiers who helped India win freedom.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is one important purpose of the National War Memorial?
options: To pay tribute to brave Indians
To show where India Gate is
To protect India's borders now
To name every Indian city
activities.explanation: The memorial pays tribute to some of the bravest Indians. It also helps us remember the cost of winning freedom.

activities.prompt: Each brick in the memorial is called a ______.
activities.hint: This word is used for the bricks that carry soldiers' names.
activities.explanation: A tablet is the name for each brick in the memorial.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the lesson with its matching detail.
activities.explanation: The pairs show what the tablets carry, where the memorial stands, and who fought for India.

activities.prompt: Put the building timeline in the correct order.
items: April 2018
The memorial is built
February 2019
activities.explanation: The building period began in April 2018 and ended in February 2019.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the memorial's tablets is correct?
options: They carry soldiers' names
They show India's borders
They name India's cities
They list the wars' weapons
activities.explanation: The tablets carry the names of soldiers who fought for India.

activities.prompt: Which idea best shows why the memorial matters?
options: It forgets the wars fought
It reminds us of freedom's cost
It replaces the work of soldiers
It marks only India's buildings
activities.explanation: The memorial reminds us of the heavy cost of winning freedom.

activities.prompt: The tablets carry soldiers' names. A child reads them quietly near India Gate. How does the child feel?
options: They feel solemn because the names show brave sacrifices.
They feel excited because many names make a game.
They feel bored because the names have no meaning.
They feel angry because the names stop their walking.

why.They feel excited because many names mak: They think many names make the memorial visit fun.
why.They feel bored because the names have n: They think the names do not connect to bravery or freedom.
why.They feel angry because the names stop t: They think a tablet's name is meant to block their path.

activities.explanation: The names remind them of soldiers and their heavy sacrifices.

activities.prompt: India fought several wars to protect its borders. A guide pauses at a soldier's tablet. Why?
options: To remember the soldier's brave service and sacrifice.
To choose the best place for a school picnic.
To plan the next war beside India's borders.
To measure how long India's wars lasted.

why.To choose the best place for a school pi: The child mistakes a memorial visit for an outing place.
why.To plan the next war beside India's bord: The child mistakes the guide for someone planning future wars.
The child thinks the guide is comparing the lengths of wars.

activities.explanation: The pause shows respect for the soldier's brave sacrifice.

activities.prompt: The memorial pays tribute to some of the bravest Indians. What does “pays tribute” mean here?
options: It means showing honour for the soldiers' bravery.
It means counting all the wars fought by India.
It means naming the people who built each tablet.
It means measuring the space used by the memorial.

why.It means counting all the wars fought by: This mistakes counting wars for honouring brave soldiers.
why.It means naming the people who built eac: This mistakes the tablet names for names of builders.
why.It means measuring the space used by the: This mistakes measuring space for honouring bravery.

activities.explanation: This meaning shows honour, which matches the memorial's purpose.

activities.prompt: The memorial reminds us of the heavy cost of winning freedom. What does “remembrance” mean here?
options: It means keeping the memory of soldiers and their sacrifices.
It means forgetting the danger faced by Indian borders.
It means calculating how many tablets the memorial holds.
It means choosing another place to fight India's wars.

why.It means calculating how many tablets th: This mistakes counting tablets for remembering those who fought.
why.It means choosing another place to fight: This mistakes choosing war sites for honouring freedom's cost.

activities.explanation: This matches remembering the soldiers and their heavy sacrifices.

They blame the medal because freedom had no cost.
They count it only as another tablet at the memorial.

why.They blame the medal because freedom had: This misreads the medal as something to blame.
why.They count it only as another tablet at: This confuses a gallantry medal with a name tablet.

activities.explanation: This honours bravery, which is what the medal recognises.

activities.title: Ekka’s Courage at Gangasagar
activities.body: Ekka showed great courage at Gangasagar on the eastern front. He attacked an enemy position that was strongly fortified. Troops faced heavy shelling and small-arms fire. Ekka charged a bunker, silenced a machine gun, and threw a grenade through its loophole. Badly wounded, he kept fighting beside his comrades. He entered the bunker and silenced another machine gun. He died after the objective was captured.
keyPoints: Ekka attacked a fortified enemy position at Gangasagar.
He silenced two machine guns.
He kept fighting despite being badly wounded.
activities.explanation: Ekka acted bravely and kept helping his comrades despite danger and injuries.

activities.prompt: A machine gun is causing heavy casualties. Its bunker is strongly fortified. What should Ekka do next?

He charges the bunker without caring for safety, because stopping it can protect his comrades.
Though badly wounded, he crawls forward and throws a grenade through the loophole, because he must reach the second gun.
He helps capture the objective, so his courage succeeds although he later dies from his injuries.

activities.title: Match Ekka’s Actions
activities.prompt: Match each action with its result.
pairs: Threw a grenade through the bunker's loophole
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an action Ekka took and its result.

activities.title: Ekka’s Bold Actions
activities.prompt: Put Ekka’s actions in the correct order.
items: He noticed the machine gun.
He charged the enemy bunker.
He silenced the machine gun.
He threw a grenade through the loophole.
He entered the bunker and silenced the second machine gun.
activities.explanation: Ekka noticed the machine gun, charged the bunker, and silenced both guns.

activities.title: Why Did Ekka Crawl Forward?
activities.prompt: Why did Ekka crawl forward?
options: To throw a grenade through the loophole.
To carry his comrades towards safety.
To repair the enemy machine gun.
To ask the enemy for a truce.
activities.explanation: Ekka crawled forward and threw a grenade through the bunker’s loophole.

activities.title: Why Was Ekka’s Courage Extraordinary?
activities.prompt: Why was Ekka’s continued fighting especially remarkable?
options: He continued fighting after being badly wounded.
He fought only after the objective was captured.
He stopped beside comrades after heavy shelling.
He entered the bunker without any weapon.
activities.explanation: He was badly wounded, yet he continued fighting beside his comrades.

activities.prompt: Ekka charged a strongly fortified bunker. Heavy fire was coming from the enemy. What did his choice show about his courage?
options: He valued the goal more than his own safety.
He believed the bunker was completely empty.
He wanted the enemy to know his name.
He planned to leave his comrades behind.

why.He believed the bunker was completely em: This mistake mistakes courage for ignorance about danger.
This mistake assumes the attack was about personal fame.
This mistake confuses courage with abandoning comrades.

activities.explanation: This is right because Ekka risked his life to help his comrades.

activities.prompt: The enemy bunker had a machine gun causing heavy casualties. Ekka saw this. What was his likely reason for charging?
options: He wanted to stop the machine gun from harming more troops.
He wanted to capture the strongest gun for himself.
He needed more bullets before he could attack.
He thought the machine gun had already stopped firing.

why.He wanted to capture the strongest gun f: This mistake assumes greed was stronger than his concern for comrades.
why.He needed more bullets before he could a: This mistake assumes he needed ammunition before acting.
why.He thought the machine gun had already s: This mistake assumes he had not noticed the firing.

activities.explanation: This is right because the gun was causing casualties and Ekka silenced it.

activities.prompt: Ekka was badly wounded during the attack. He still fought beside his comrades. How might he have felt?
options: Focused on helping his comrades, despite the pain.
Ready to stop as soon as he felt pain.
Confused about why his comrades were fighting.
Angry that the objective had been captured.

This mistake assumes pain made him give up immediately.
why.Confused about why his comrades were fig: This mistake assumes he did not understand the shared fight.
why.Angry that the objective had been captur: This mistake gives him a feeling the facts do not support.

activities.explanation: This is right because he kept helping his comrades despite severe pain.

activities.prompt: Ekka crawled forward after being wounded. He threw a grenade through a bunker loophole. Why crawl instead of charge?
options: His wounds made standing and running very hard.
He wanted to show the enemy that he feared nothing.
He thought a grenade needed extra running speed.
He planned to enter without using the grenade.

why.He wanted to show the enemy that he fear: This mistake assumes crawling showed fear instead of determination.
why.He thought a grenade needed extra runnin: This mistake wrongly links crawling speed to throwing the grenade.
why.He planned to enter without using the gr: This mistake assumes the grenade had no part in his attack.

activities.explanation: This is right because his severe wounds likely made fast movement difficult.

activities.prompt: The enemy position was strongly fortified. A school play fort has thick walls all around. What does ‘fortified’ mean here?
options: Protected by strong walls and defenses.
Designed mainly for children to play.
Left open so any soldier could enter.
Used only for keeping small toys.

This mistake uses the play-fort example to confuse two meanings.
This mistake gives fortified the opposite meaning.
This mistake mistakes a strong defense for toy storage.

activities.explanation: This is right because fortified means protected by strong defenses.

activities.prompt: Ekka silenced both machine guns, and then the objective was captured. What can we work out?
options: Stopping the guns helped his side capture the objective.
The objective was captured before the guns were silenced.
The guns were the only enemies at the position.
Taking the objective made every enemy weapon stop.

why.The objective was captured before the gu: This mistake reverses the order of the events.
why.The guns were the only enemies at the po: This mistake assumes there were no other enemies present.
why.Taking the objective made every enemy we: This mistake confuses the captured objective with every weapon stopping.

activities.explanation: This is right because silencing the guns helped his side take the objective.
